about: The bad and good example for each rule: the migration body that trips the rule, the migration body that does the same job safely, and one line naming what separates them. The example teaches the shape; the fixture pair proves it. Every text and every snippet is written for this package — the facts an operation exhibits are free, the wording and the code are not, and nothing here is lifted from another tool's or the database's documentation. Snippets are Laravel migration bodies, kept short and runnable, and a completeness test parses each one so an example that would not compile never ships. Entries are keyed and sorted by rule id. An entry may also carry `false_positives`: where the rule knowingly reports something a careful reader would not. That is governance rather than decoration — a rule whose author never wrote down when it cries wolf has not finished thinking about it, and the first person to meet the false positive is a user who then stops trusting the whole tool. It is optional in the reader and mandatory where a driver's completeness gate says so.

DEPLOY.LEGACY.CONSTRAINT_NOT_ENFORCED.note: NOT ENFORCED is a constraint MySQL stores and never applies. Unlike PostgreSQL's NOT VALID it is not a step toward enforcement: nothing completes it later except ALTER TABLE ... ALTER CHECK ... ENFORCED, and that fails unless the rows already satisfy the rule. So the finding is usually about data rather than schema — something violated the check, somebody switched it off, and the table has claimed the rule ever since.
DEPLOY.LEGACY.CONSTRAINT_NOT_ENFORCED.false_positives: A check kept NOT ENFORCED as documentation — a rule the team states but cannot apply to historical rows — is reported the same way. The catalog holds ENFORCED = NO and nothing else, so no field separates a deliberate one from a forgotten one, and the check reports the state without guessing which it is.

DEPLOY.LEGACY.CONSTRAINT_NOT_VALIDATED.note: NOT VALID is the right way to add a constraint to a table that is in use — it skips the scan of existing rows and holds its lock for a moment rather than for minutes. It is half the job: until VALIDATE CONSTRAINT runs, the constraint holds for new rows and says nothing about the old ones, so a reader who trusts it is trusting half of it. Validate in the same migration on a small table, in a follow-up on a large one.
DEPLOY.LEGACY.CONSTRAINT_NOT_VALIDATED.false_positives: A constraint left NOT VALID on purpose is reported the same way. A team that added it to stop new bad rows while a back-fill runs is doing exactly the right thing, and this check cannot see the back-fill — it reports the state and never guesses whether the validation is planned.

GEN.L1.DML_WITHOUT_WHERE.good:
// Scope the write, and for a large table delete in bounded batches:
DB::table('audit_log')->where('created_at', '<', now()->subDays(30))->limit(1000)->delete();
GEN.L1.DML_WITHOUT_WHERE.note: An UPDATE or DELETE with no WHERE changes or removes every row; a forgotten predicate turns a targeted fix into a whole-table sweep. Add the WHERE you meant — and for a large table, batch the write so it does not lock every row at once.
GEN.L1.DML_WITHOUT_WHERE.false_positives: A whole-table write that was MEANT is reported, because a forgotten predicate and a deliberately absent one are the same statement: seeding a lookup table, or back-filling a new column across every row, both arrive here. Declaring the intent with #[SqlensAllowDestructive] does not silence the finding — it becomes a named suppression carrying its reason, so the sweep stays visible. Nothing with a WHERE is reported at all, including one whose predicate is a sub-select that matches every row, so the rule under-reports rather than over-reports on that side.

GEN.L1.DOWN_MORE_DESTRUCTIVE.good:
// down() undoes exactly what up() did, and nothing beside it:
Schema::table('orders', fn (Blueprint $table) => $table->dropColumn('status'));
GEN.L1.DOWN_MORE_DESTRUCTIVE.note: A rollback is run at the worst possible moment — a deploy that is already going wrong — and this one takes away data the migration never added. Make down() the exact inverse of up(). If part of the change genuinely cannot be undone, throw from down() with that reason rather than destroying something adjacent to make the schema look right.
GEN.L1.DOWN_MORE_DESTRUCTIVE.false_positives: A deliberately consolidating migration — one whose down() also removes tables an earlier migration created — is reported, because from this migration's own statements that is indistinguishable from the mistake. What the rule does NOT report is the mirror case: a down() that drops a different column of a table up() did touch. That granularity is not available on both engines in the same way, and a rule that asked for it would flag every symmetric add/drop-column migration on one of them.

GEN.L3.DML_ON_SCHEMA_CHANGED_TABLE.note: Changing a table's schema and backfilling its data in one migration holds the schema change's lock for the whole backfill. Split them: one migration changes the schema, a later one (or a job) fills the data once the lock is released.
GEN.L3.DML_ON_SCHEMA_CHANGED_TABLE.false_positives: The cost this names is a shared lock window, and on MySQL there is none: the server commits implicitly on both sides of a DDL statement, so the schema change and the data write never sit in one transaction however the migration is configured. The finding still points at a real problem there — the two halves cannot be deployed, timed out or rolled back independently — but its reasoning about lock duration is PostgreSQL's. A migration that sets $withinTransaction = false is not reported on either engine; the rule reads that flag rather than assuming Laravel's default.

GEN.L4.DOWN_MISSING.note: Laravel rolls back by calling down(), and nothing else — an absent or empty one means the rollback silently does nothing, and the moment you need it is the moment a deploy is already going wrong. If the change genuinely cannot be undone (a dropped column's data is gone), write a down() that throws with that reason: an answer on record beats an absence, and it is the one thing a rollback must never do quietly, which is succeed without undoing anything.
GEN.L4.DOWN_MISSING.false_positives: A migration that genuinely has nothing to undo reads exactly like one whose author forgot. An empty down() and a missing one both emit no statements, and only the file separates them, so a data-only migration whose effect a rollback should KEEP is reported. What is not reported: a down() that throws with a reason — that body parses as present, which is the right answer, because an explicit refusal is a rollback path and a documented one.

MY.L1.DROP_COLUMN.note: DROP COLUMN deletes the column and its data. On MySQL it is DDL and causes an implicit commit, so the values are gone the instant the statement runs whatever fails later in the same migration; down() can add the column back but not what was in it.
MY.L1.DROP_COLUMN.false_positives: A column dropped from a table the same migration created is exempt, but one added by an earlier migration and never populated in production reads exactly like a live column here. The rule judges the statement, not the data behind it. It also cannot know that the reads were already retired in a shipped release — which is the correct sequence, and still produces a finding on the day the drop lands.

MY.L1.DROP_TABLE.good:
// A rename keeps a rollback path while the code that used the table is retired:
Schema::rename('legacy_events', 'legacy_events_deprecated');
MY.L1.DROP_TABLE.note: DROP TABLE removes the table and every row. On MySQL it is DDL and causes an implicit commit, so it is final the instant it runs - no transaction protects it, and down() can re-create the table but not its rows.
MY.L1.DROP_TABLE.false_positives: A table the migration itself created and then drops is not reported, but a scratch or import table created by an EARLIER migration is — and dropping such a table is often exactly what was meant. The rule cannot see which, because it reads one migration and not your deploy history. That case is what #[SqlensAllowDestructive] with a reason is for: it keeps the finding visible and records who decided.

MY.L1.TRUNCATE.note: TRUNCATE is DDL on MySQL, so it causes an implicit commit and cannot be rolled back: the rows are gone the instant it runs, whatever fails later in the migration. A bounded DELETE does the same job while the work is still reversible.
MY.L1.TRUNCATE.false_positives: A staging or import table that the migration itself created is not reported, but one created by an EARLIER migration is — and emptying such a table is often exactly what was meant. That case is what #[SqlensAllowDestructive] is for: it records the decision instead of hiding it.

MY.L2.COPY_ALTER_CHARSET.bad: DB::statement('ALTER TABLE orders CONVERT TO CHARACTER SET utf8mb4');
MY.L2.COPY_ALTER_CHARSET.note: CONVERT TO CHARACTER SET re-encodes every value in every string column, so InnoDB copies the whole table under a shared lock and writes queue for the entire run. Converting column by column covers less data per statement and spreads the work over several deploys.
MY.L2.COPY_ALTER_CHARSET.false_positives: The main false-positive candidate is the table DEFAULT character set, which looks almost identical and costs nothing — and it is deliberately NOT reported (measured: in place, existing rows untouched). A CONVERT TO into the character set already in place is still reported, because MySQL re-encodes every row regardless; that is a real cost, not a false positive.

MY.L2.COPY_ALTER_TYPE.note: ->change() compiles to ALTER TABLE ... MODIFY, which restates the column's whole definition; a data type change behind it rebuilds the table with ALGORITHM=COPY while writes queue. Adding a new column and backfilling it keeps the table available, and a raw statement carrying ALGORITHM=INPLACE, LOCK=NONE makes MySQL refuse an in-place change it cannot do rather than copying the table.
MY.L2.COPY_ALTER_TYPE.false_positives: The rule reports a redefinition whose only real change is the column's DEFAULT, which MySQL runs instantly. The statement gives no way to tell that case from a type change, and the trade is deliberate: a false positive costs one look at the column, a false negative costs an outage. The finding says so in its own text rather than leaving a reader to discover it.

MY.L2.FK_TARGET_NON_UNIQUE.note: MySQL 8.4 rejects a foreign key whose referenced columns no unique key covers — ERROR 6125, with restrict_fk_on_non_standard_key on by default — so the migration fails outright. A plain index is not enough; the key must be unique and cover exactly the referenced columns.
MY.L2.FK_TARGET_NON_UNIQUE.false_positives: The rule answers only when the target table is created in the same migration. The ordinary case — a foreign key into an existing table — is reported as undetermined rather than flagged, precisely because flagging every constrained() call would be crying wolf on the commonest correct migration there is.

MY.L2.NO_PRIMARY_KEY.note: An InnoDB table without a primary key makes row-based replication scan the whole table for every row it applies, and every online schema-change tool refuses to work on it. Give the table a key when you create it — $table->id(), or $table->primary([...]) for a natural composite one; adding it later rebuilds the whole table.
MY.L2.NO_PRIMARY_KEY.false_positives: A deliberately keyless log or staging table is a real case and is reported. It is handled with a baseline entry, a config ignore or an annotation rather than by weakening the rule, because a rule loose enough to miss it would also miss the tables that matter. A table with a UNIQUE key but no primary key is NOT flagged — it is reported as undetermined, since InnoDB may promote that index to the clustered one.

MY.L3.ALGORITHM_LOCK_UNEXPRESSIBLE.note: Laravel's schema builder has no way to emit ALGORITHM= or LOCK=, so an operation MySQL will not run online takes whatever algorithm the server picks. Writing it as a raw statement that names both makes the outcome certain — the server refuses instead of copying the table behind your back — and the comment keeps raw SQL a deliberate exception rather than a habit.
MY.L3.ALGORITHM_LOCK_UNEXPRESSIBLE.false_positives: It suggests rather than judges, so its silences are not passes: an operation the server runs online, or one the matrix cannot classify, gets no suggestion. The reportable false positive is a team that has decided to accept whatever algorithm MySQL picks — for them every non-online operation carries a hint they will not act on, which is what the level gate and a config ignore are for.

MY.L3.EXCHANGE_PARTITION_CLAUSE_IGNORED.bad: DB::statement('ALTER TABLE orders ALGORITHM=INPLACE, LOCK=NONE, EXCHANGE PARTITION p2025 WITH TABLE orders_2025');
MY.L3.EXCHANGE_PARTITION_CLAUSE_IGNORED.good: DB::statement('ALTER TABLE orders EXCHANGE PARTITION p2025 WITH TABLE orders_2025');
MY.L3.EXCHANGE_PARTITION_CLAUSE_IGNORED.note: MySQL parses ALGORITHM= and LOCK= on an EXCHANGE PARTITION and acts on neither. Measured on 8.4.10: ALGORITHM=COPY with LOCK=NONE is a contradiction the server rejects with error 1846 on ADD COLUMN, ADD INDEX and DROP PARTITION alike -- and accepts here. The clause is therefore a promise nothing kept, and the silence is indistinguishable from agreement.
MY.L3.EXCHANGE_PARTITION_CLAUSE_IGNORED.false_positives: The same clause on ADD, DROP, TRUNCATE, REORGANIZE or COALESCE PARTITION is validated by the server and is not reported -- writing it there is correct. An EXCHANGE without the clause is not reported either: it made no promise to break. A string literal spelling the clause never decides the verdict, in either direction.

MY.L3.MISSING_LOCK_WAIT_TIMEOUT.note: The bound is what turns a stuck deploy into a fast failure. It does not make the change succeed, so decide beforehand what happens on a timeout — retrying when the table is quieter, rather than raising the value back toward the unbounded default. innodb_lock_wait_timeout bounds row locks and does not help here; max_execution_time applies to read-only SELECT statements and does not reach a schema change at all.
MY.L3.MISSING_LOCK_WAIT_TIMEOUT.false_positives: A project that sets `lock_wait_timeout` OUTSIDE the migration — in the connection's PDO options, as a server default, or from a deploy wrapper — is already bounded and is still reported here. A static reader sees only the migration's own statements, and inferring the rest would mean guessing at a connection it never opens. The counterpart is also true and is why the rule reads the whole stream rather than the line above: a preamble at the top of `up()` counts for every statement that follows it.

MY.L3.MIXED_DDL_DML_NOT_ATOMIC.bad:
Schema::table('orders', fn (Blueprint $table) => $table->string('status')->nullable());
DB::statement("UPDATE orders SET status = 'new' WHERE status IS NULL");
MY.L3.MIXED_DDL_DML_NOT_ATOMIC.note: Every MySQL DDL statement causes an implicit commit, so a migration that changes the schema and then writes data is not one operation: if the write fails, the schema change is already permanent and nothing rolls back. Split them so each step either completes or leaves nothing behind.
MY.L3.MIXED_DDL_DML_NOT_ATOMIC.false_positives: A migration that writes data it can safely re-run — an idempotent backfill, or one seeding a table the same migration created — is still reported, because the statement stream cannot show idempotence. The finding is about recoverability, so a team that has satisfied itself the write is replayable is right to suppress it with a recorded reason.

MY.L4.DROP_WITHOUT_DEPLOY_WINDOW.good:
// Deploy 1: ship code that no longer reads legacy_events. Nothing here.
// Deploy 2 (a LATER migration): the drop, once no running version references it.
MY.L4.DROP_WITHOUT_DEPLOY_WINDOW.note: A drop breaks any still-running old application version that references the object. Make it the contract half of an expand/contract: one deploy stops using it, a later deploy removes it. Level 1 asks whether the data is expendable; this level asks whether anyone is still reading.
MY.L4.DROP_WITHOUT_DEPLOY_WINDOW.false_positives: The object may already be unreferenced — the reads retired three releases ago and nobody removed the table until now. SQLens reads the SQL and not your application, so it cannot tell that case from a genuine window violation. It is heuristic for exactly this reason, and #[SqlensAllowDestructive] with a reason is how you record that the window is already closed.

MY.L4.ENUM_CHANGE.note: MySQL stores an ENUM value as its ordinal, so removing, reordering or renaming a member changes what existing rows mean to an application that has not been redeployed — and a rename does it instantly, with no lock and no rewrite to notice. Appending at the end is the only change that leaves every stored value meaning what it did.
MY.L4.ENUM_CHANGE.false_positives: An append-only change is reported too, because the statement names the whole member list and not the delta — the rule cannot tell an append from an insertion without the live column. The trade is deliberate: a false positive costs one look at the column, a false negative ships an application reading a value the database no longer has.

MY.L4.EXPAND_WITHOUT_CONTRACT.note: Adding a column and filling it from data that is already there is the expand step of an expand/contract deploy on MySQL. It is correct, and it is half of a plan: until the contract step runs, the table holds two columns for one fact and nothing in the schema says which is authoritative. Nothing breaks, which is exactly why the second half is the one that gets forgotten. Drop the replaced column once every deployed reader has stopped using it.
MY.L4.EXPAND_WITHOUT_CONTRACT.false_positives: A column added for genuinely new data is not reported, because the rule requires a back-fill from the rows that already exist — that write is the evidence, not the name of the column. The reverse gap is real and deliberate: a back-fill that runs in a queued job instead of the migration is invisible, so a genuine expand/contract done that way is NOT flagged. And on the single-file fast path a contract step in another migration is out of view, so a finished sequence can read as unfinished — the same limit every run-wide question has there. MySQL-specific: CHANGE, MODIFY and RENAME COLUMN are never reported, because each alters a column in place and no second column ever exists — there is nothing for a contract step to remove.

MY.L4.IDENTIFIER_LENGTH.note: Nothing here is over 64 characters. The table is 32 characters and the two columns 25 and 24 — and the index name Laravel derives from all three is 89. MySQL refuses that statement with `ERROR 1059` and the deploy stops, which is the good failure mode: loud, immediate, in front of somebody who can act. The rule's job is to move it from the deploy to the diff. The limit is measured in CHARACTERS here, not bytes — the same 32 two-byte characters PostgreSQL truncates are accepted by MySQL without complaint.
MY.L4.IDENTIFIER_LENGTH.false_positives: An identifier that is long on purpose and stays inside the limit — the rule measures, it does not judge style, so a 60-character name is never reported. What it cannot see is a name assembled at runtime by code the migration calls: the rule reads the statement the schema builder compiled, so anything built after that point is outside its reach on both engines.

MY.L5.COLLATION_MIXED.note: MySQL cannot compare two strings under different collations, so it converts the side with the lower coercibility at runtime — and a converted column can no longer be answered from its own index. The parent lookup that was a B-tree descent becomes a scan of the child table, and nothing in the query says so: EXPLAIN shows the missing index and not the reason for it. Measured on 8.4.10, the server refuses to CREATE such a key at all (error 3780) even with foreign_key_checks off, so the state arrives only by altering a column's collation on a table that already has the constraint while the checks are down — what a restore script or a charset sweep does. Nothing reports the result afterwards.
MY.L5.COLLATION_MIXED.false_positives: A _bin or _cs collation differing from its table is a decision, not a leftover: a hash, a token, a base64 payload or a case-sensitive technical key is stored that way on purpose, and unifying it would collapse the distinction the column exists for. Those are never reported. An edge pointing at a table outside the audited scope is answered undetermined rather than guessed, because an edge nobody followed and an edge that matched look identical from inside the schema that was read.

MY.L5.FK_NULLABLE_IN_UNIQUE.note: A unique key over (team_id, member_id) reads as "one row per pair", and under the default NULL treatment it is not enforced for any row whose member_id is NULL. Measured on PostgreSQL 18.4 and MySQL 8.4 alike: three rows sharing a team_id and carrying a NULL member_id all insert. The constraint holds for exactly the rows that never needed it. A key made entirely of foreign-key columns is a relationship, and a relationship with a missing side is not one. MySQL has no NULLS NOT DISTINCT, so NOT NULL is the fix — or, where the column must stay optional, a stored generated column carrying a sentinel with the unique key over that.
MY.L5.FK_NULLABLE_IN_UNIQUE.false_positives: Cut narrow on purpose, because a nullable foreign key is usually correct. Nothing is reported unless the column sits inside a unique key of at least TWO columns whose every member is itself a foreign-key column. A single-column nullable unique key is the optional-one-to-one idiom (profile_id UNIQUE NULL, superseded_by_id UNIQUE NULL) and works precisely because NULLs are distinct; a key mixing a foreign key with a payload column is the application's own uniqueness rule and whether a NULL belongs in it is a domain question. The nullable PRIMARY KEY case the design started from is absent because it is unreachable: PostgreSQL refuses it outright and MySQL rewrites it.

MY.L5.FLOAT_MONEY.note: A binary float cannot represent 0.10 exactly, so ten of them do not add up to 1.00 — near enough that every screen shows 1.00 and every comparison against it fails. The error surfaces as one cent on a statement months after the schema decision, and whoever finds it has no way back to the column. decimal()/numeric stores the digits, so the arithmetic is the arithmetic of the invoice.
MY.L5.FLOAT_MONEY.false_positives: Nothing in a catalog says a column holds money, so the trigger is a heuristic on the NAME and says so in the finding itself. The dictionary splits terms by confidence for exactly this reason: a strong term (price, invoice_total, rechnungsbetrag) reports on its own, while a weak one (rate, value, wert, total) is ordinary language that is only sometimes money and needs a second, STRUCTURAL signal — a sibling currency column, or a cents segment in the name. A suffix of _amount is deliberately not such a signal, because amount is itself a weak term and would be vouching for itself. A project tunes both directions through sqlens.audit.money_columns.extra and .ignore.

MY.L5.SQL_MODE_DIVISION_BY_ZERO_SILENT.note: The flag this rule requires is ERROR_FOR_DIVISION_BY_ZERO. Division by zero yields NULL instead of raising. A NULL flowing into an average, a ratio or a money column reads as missing data rather than as a defect, so it survives review and lands in a report somebody trusts.
MY.L5.SQL_MODE_DIVISION_BY_ZERO_SILENT.false_positives: An application that handles the NULL deliberately — COALESCE around every division, or a schema where the divisor cannot be zero — is the expected exception. Only the server value is judged.

MY.L5.SQL_MODE_NOT_STRICT.note: The flag this rule requires is STRICT_TRANS_TABLES. Without it an out-of-range number, an over-long string or an invalid date is truncated and the INSERT reports success with a warning nobody reads. The application believes it stored what it sent, and the shortened value is found later by whoever notices the data is wrong — which is the most expensive shape a defect can have: a successful statement.
MY.L5.SQL_MODE_NOT_STRICT.false_positives: A project that has deliberately accepted lax inserts on a legacy schema is the expected exception and belongs on the ignore list with the reason recorded there. Only the SERVER value is judged: Laravel sets sql_mode per connection from the strict flag, so an application connection can be strict while everything else that connects to the same server is not.

MY.L6.CHARACTER_SET_SERVER_NOT_UTF8MB4.note: Laravel's schema builder emits an explicit CHARACTER SET for the tables it creates, so the common failure is not those tables — it is everything else: a database an operator created by hand, a table added by hand, a raw-SQL migration. Those take the server default, and on latin1 they silently cannot hold most of Unicode. Depending on the SQL mode MySQL replaces the character or truncates the value at it rather than refusing the write, so the row is stored, altered, and nobody finds out until somebody asks why their name is wrong.
MY.L6.CHARACTER_SET_SERVER_NOT_UTF8MB4.false_positives: The COLLATION within utf8mb4 is deliberately not judged: utf8mb4_0900_ai_ci and utf8mb4_unicode_ci are both legitimate, and the second pins an older Unicode version, which is a real reason on a database that must keep sort order stable across an upgrade. Nor is collation_server judged as its own finding — measured on 8.4.10, MySQL will not let the two disagree: setting character_set_server to latin1 moved collation_server to latin1_swedish_ci by itself, and setting collation_server to utf8mb4_unicode_ci moved character_set_server to utf8mb4. Two rules would report one misconfiguration twice, and an ignore entry for one would leave the other shouting.

MY.L6.CHARSET_NOT_UTF8MB4.note: utf8mb3 is three bytes per character, which is exactly the Basic Multilingual Plane and nothing beyond it — every emoji is outside, and so is a good deal of CJK. The name is the trap: it says utf8 and it is not. Depending on the SQL mode MySQL replaces the character or truncates the value at it rather than refusing the write, so the row is stored, altered, and nobody finds out until somebody asks why their name is wrong. MySQL 8.4 deprecates utf8mb3 on top of that.
MY.L6.CHARSET_NOT_UTF8MB4.false_positives: A column that will only ever hold ASCII — a country code, a base64 token, a hex digest — loses nothing by being narrow, and converting it costs a table copy for no gain. The binary character set is never reported: a VARBINARY column holds bytes rather than text, and demanding utf8mb4 of it would be advice that breaks the column.

MY.L6.COLLATION_LEGACY.note: utf8mb4_general_ci predates MySQL 8.0 and does not implement the Unicode Collation Algorithm: it compares by a shortened table that treats whole groups of characters as equal. It does not merely sort differently from what a reader expects — for several languages it sorts wrongly, and it reports characters as equal that a user would not. utf8mb4_0900_ai_ci implements UCA 9.0.0 and has been the server default since 8.0.
MY.L6.COLLATION_LEGACY.false_positives: A _bin or _cs collation on a hash, a token or a case-sensitive technical key is a decision rather than a leftover, and is never reported. Neither are the language-specific 0900 collations such as utf8mb4_de_pb_0900_ai_ci — they are the modern family. Before converting, check the unique indexes: a new collation changes what counts as equal, so rows that have always coexisted can collide during the ALTER and fail it on data nobody touched.

MY.L6.DEFAULT_STORAGE_ENGINE_NOT_INNODB.note: A table created without an explicit ENGINE takes the server default. Under MyISAM it has no transactions, no foreign keys and no crash recovery — and none of those absences raise anything: a migration wrapped in a transaction simply does not roll back, a foreign key is silently not enforced, and an unclean shutdown leaves the table needing repair. Laravel's schema builder emits ENGINE only when database.connections.mysql.engine is configured, which is not the default, so the server value usually decides.
MY.L6.DEFAULT_STORAGE_ENGINE_NOT_INNODB.false_positives: A deliberately mixed engine landscape is rare and belongs on the ignore list with the reason recorded there. There is also a case that is neither a finding nor silence: a server whose default is MyISAM while disabled_storage_engines refuses MyISAM outright. The setting looks wrong and cannot take effect, so the rule reports a PASS with that reason — reporting nothing would be indistinguishable from a rule that never ran, and reporting a failure would send somebody to change a setting that is already harmless.

MY.L6.EXPLICIT_DEFAULTS_FOR_TIMESTAMP_OF.note: The example is server configuration because that is where the value lives — no migration can set it, and the server applies its consequences at table-creation time, so none of the migrations anybody reviews shows what happened. With it off the first TIMESTAMP column in a table silently gains DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP ON UPDATE CURRENT_TIMESTAMP and rewrites itself on every UPDATE, and assigning NULL to a TIMESTAMP column stores the current time rather than raising. The second is the expensive one: a column holding "now" because the application wrote null is indistinguishable, in the data, from one it filled deliberately.
MY.L6.EXPLICIT_DEFAULTS_FOR_TIMESTAMP_OF.false_positives: A deployment that deliberately keeps the legacy behavior to support code written against it is the expected exception and belongs on the ignore list with the reason recorded there. The check reads the server's value and never the reading session's, so a connection that set the flag for itself is not reported as a server finding. Both spellings are accepted: MySQL reports this value differently depending on how it is asked. Measured on 8.4.10: performance_schema.global_variables and SHOW GLOBAL VARIABLES both answer ON, while @@global.explicit_defaults_for_timestamp answers 1. The reader takes the performance_schema path normally and the SHOW path when that schema is unavailable, so both of ITS paths yield the word — but the matrix expectation, an operator's my.cnf and any hand-written comparison may all carry the digit. Treating the two as different values would flag a correctly configured server.

MY.L6.INNODB_ROW_FORMAT_NOT_DYNAMIC.note: Laravel's schema builder never emits an explicit ROW_FORMAT, so every table it creates takes the server default. Under COMPACT or REDUNDANT that means the 767-byte index key prefix limit instead of 3072 — 191 characters at utf8mb4 — and the first unique index on a VARCHAR(255) aborts with ERROR 1071. The timing is what costs: it aborts mid-deploy, leaving some migrations applied and some not, on a server every other check called healthy. The workaround everyone reaches for, Schema::defaultStringLength(191), converts a one-line server fix into a permanent narrowing of every string column in the application, invisible to whoever reads the migrations later.
MY.L6.INNODB_ROW_FORMAT_NOT_DYNAMIC.false_positives: A server correctly handing out DYNAMIC while the catalog still holds tables created years ago under an older default is NOT reported here. There is nothing in the configuration to fix, and reporting it would send a reader to a file that is already correct while never naming the actual work — an ALTER TABLE ... ROW_FORMAT=DYNAMIC rebuild per table. That is a statement about the schema rather than the server. Only the server's value is judged, and the comparison folds case: MySQL reports the value lower-case while every config file and the manual write it upper-case, so a strict comparison would flag the exact value the matrix asks for.

MY.L6.LOWER_CASE_TABLE_NAMES_RISK.bad:
CREATE TABLE Orders (id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY);
-- on a server initialized with lower_case_table_names = 0
MY.L6.LOWER_CASE_TABLE_NAMES_RISK.good: CREATE TABLE orders (id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY);
MY.L6.LOWER_CASE_TABLE_NAMES_RISK.note: The classic development-against-production split. A macOS install initializes with 2 and a Linux server with 0, so a migration using mixed-case names passes on one and fails on the other — and nothing in the migration says which. The value is fixed when the server is initialized and cannot be changed afterwards; moving it means a new server and a dump/reload, which is why the finding proposes consistent lower-case naming rather than a setting to flip.
MY.L6.LOWER_CASE_TABLE_NAMES_RISK.false_positives: SQLens has no opinion about the right value and never asserts one — 0 is right on Linux, 2 is what macOS installs. The expectation trigger fires only against sqlens.audit.expect.lower_case_table_names, which is a project statement and is unset by default, so a project that has never cared sees nothing. The second trigger needs no statement and is objectively provable: on a case-sensitive server (0) a schema that already holds mixed-case table names is one where a query writing a different case will not find them. A catalog that could not be read is undetermined rather than clean.

MY.L6.PK_NOT_BIGINT.note: increments() gives a 4-byte auto-incrementing key that runs out at 2,147,483,647, with no warning on the way there — the first symptom is an INSERT failing on a table that has worked for years. id() gives a bigint. The fix is due exactly when it is most expensive, because widening the key rewrites the table and every index over it, under a lock, on your largest table.
MY.L6.PK_NOT_BIGINT.false_positives: A small lookup table will never approach the ceiling, and widening its key buys nothing. Ignore those deliberately rather than widening every table in the schema. Composite and non-integer keys are not reported at all: a composite key's range is the product of its parts, so "too narrow" stops being a property of one column.

MY.L6.SQL_MODE_ENGINE_SUBSTITUTION.note: The flag this rule requires is NO_ENGINE_SUBSTITUTION. A table asking for an engine the server cannot provide silently gets the default one. The migration succeeds, the table exists, and it may have neither transactions nor foreign keys — none of which the schema file mentions.
MY.L6.SQL_MODE_ENGINE_SUBSTITUTION.false_positives: A deployment that deliberately substitutes engines, for instance while migrating storage engines in stages, is the expected exception. Only the server value is judged.

MY.L6.SQL_MODE_LOOSE_GROUP_BY.note: The flag this rule requires is ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY. A GROUP BY may select a column that is neither grouped nor aggregated, and the server returns an arbitrary row's value for it — not random enough to notice in development, not stable enough to rely on.
MY.L6.SQL_MODE_LOOSE_GROUP_BY.false_positives: A codebase carrying queries written against the loose behavior is the expected exception, and turning the flag on would break them rather than fix them — which is why this is an idiom finding rather than a safety one. It belongs on the ignore list with a note about the migration owed.

MY.L6.TIME_ZONE_NOT_UTC.note: SYSTEM is MySQL's shipped default and means "whatever the host's clock is set to", which makes the database's behavior a property of the machine rather than of a decision. Measured on a real 8.4 running SYSTEM: CONVERT_TZ('2026-01-01 14:00:00','SYSTEM','+00:00') returned 13:00:00 — the server silently used the host's offset, without raising and without warning. The offset form is preferred over the named UTC because it works on every server: the named spellings need the timezone tables loaded, and on the same server with mysql.time_zone_name empty, CONVERT_TZ('2026-01-01 14:00:00','UTC','+00:00') returned NULL while the pure-offset conversion returned a value.
MY.L6.TIME_ZONE_NOT_UTC.false_positives: Three configurations are correct and stay silent: the offset form +00:00, and the named forms UTC and Etc/UTC, which is what a managed host with tzdata loaded reports. GMT, Etc/GMT, Universal and Zulu are deliberately NOT accepted — the same instant but a different statement of intent, and the next person to touch a server set to GMT may well "correct" it to a local zone. Only the server's value is judged: Laravel sets the session timezone from the connection config on every connection it opens, so a session running something else is the framework's choice and not a server finding.

MY.L6.TIME_ZONE_TABLES_EMPTY.bad:
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM mysql.time_zone_name;
-- 0, while @@global.time_zone names a zone
MY.L6.TIME_ZONE_TABLES_EMPTY.good:
-- run once, as an administrator, against the server's own tzdata:
--   mysql_tzinfo_to_sql /usr/share/zoneinfo | mysql -u root mysql
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM mysql.time_zone_name;
-- a few hundred
MY.L6.TIME_ZONE_TABLES_EMPTY.note: A fresh MySQL install ships mysql.time_zone_name EMPTY; it is populated by running mysql_tzinfo_to_sql. Measured on a real 8.4 with the tables empty, CONVERT_TZ('2026-01-01 14:00:00','UTC','+00:00') returns NULL rather than raising — a query that looks correct silently produces nothing. Also measured: with the tables empty the server REFUSES to adopt a named zone, answering ERROR 1298. So this state does not arise by setting the value; it arises when a server that HAD the tables loses them — a mysql-schema restore that omitted them, an upgrade that did not re-import, an image rebuilt without the step.
MY.L6.TIME_ZONE_TABLES_EMPTY.false_positives: An offset value (+00:00, -05:30) is resolved arithmetically and SYSTEM defers to the host clock — neither touches the tables, and neither is reported. That is the whole FP surface: the rule fires only where the dependency actually exists. A server whose tables cannot be READ at all is undetermined rather than a finding; on a managed database the mysql schema is commonly out of reach, and 'we could not look' is not 'they are empty'.

MY.L7.INDEX_REDUNDANT.note: A b-tree index on (customer_id) answers nothing the index on (customer_id, placed_at) cannot: order is the fact, and the wider index serves every lookup the narrower one does. The narrow one is still maintained on every insert and on every update that touches its column, occupies its own pages in cache, and is one more relation to vacuum — for no read it serves alone.
MY.L7.INDEX_REDUNDANT.false_positives: The comparison is only made between indexes the reading already judged comparable, because a naive left-prefix test is wrong on the first real schema it meets and wrong in the direction that advises a DROP. A partial index, an expression or functional index, a non-default operator class, a prefix-length key and any method other than b-tree are each excluded with a NAMED skip, so a schema full of them is told they were not compared rather than handed a clean report. A unique index or primary key is never reported as the victim — dropping it changes what the schema ALLOWS, not what it costs — though it may still be the index that covers another. An index carrying an INCLUDE payload is never the victim either: measured, (a) INCLUDE (b) and (a) report the SAME key columns, so without that flag the rule would recommend dropping the more useful of the two.

MY.L7.INDEX_UNUSED.note: An index nobody reads is still written on every insert and on every update touching its columns, occupies its own pages in cache, and on PostgreSQL is one more relation for vacuum to walk. The read side gains nothing. The counter says how often it has been scanned; the window says whether that number means anything. MySQL keeps these counters in performance_schema, which can be switched off entirely, and records no reset point at all — so the window length is permanently unknown on this engine.
MY.L7.INDEX_UNUSED.false_positives: This rule is EXPERIMENTAL and opt-in, and the reason is not immaturity: its verdict depends on WHEN it is asked, which is a direct tension with the package's determinism promise. Three things the counter cannot see. Statistics are per INSTANCE, so an index read only on a replica looks unused on the primary. A query that runs monthly has not run yet if the window is shorter than a month, which is why the minimum window is configurable and defaults to 30 days. And a counter that was reset yesterday says nothing at all — that case is undetermined with a named reason, never a pass and never a finding. A primary key or unique index is never reported: it exists to refuse a write, and it has been doing that silently the whole time. On MySQL the answer is undetermined unless min_observation_days is set to 0, because the engine keeps no equivalent of stats_reset and the window's length cannot be established.

MY.L7.UNBATCHED_MASS_DML.note: A write with a predicate but no bound runs as one statement over every row it matches, holding row locks for the whole of it while the migration blocks the deploy. Bound it with a LIMIT or a key range — or, for a large table, move the backfill into a queued job so a deploy is not waiting on it.
MY.L7.UNBATCHED_MASS_DML.false_positives: This is a heuristic and says so in the finding: it can see that a statement is unbounded, never how many rows that means, and it never asks the server for a row count. On a small lookup table an unbounded write is a non-event and is still reported — which is why the rule sits at level 7, the band a project turns on when it wants estimates as well as facts. It is lenient in the other direction too: a BETWEEN silences it, because a key-range walk is the fix it recommends, and a BETWEEN on a non-key column bounds nothing.

MY.L8.FK_ID_SUFFIX.note: Laravel derives a relation's foreign key from the related model — `author_id` for a `User` — so `belongsTo(User::class)` resolves without being told anything. Name the column `author` and every relation on that side has to pass the key explicitly, in code nobody re-checks when the schema moves. The rule identifies the column from the CONSTRAINT, never from its name: a rule that looked for `_id` would find only the columns that already satisfy it.
MY.L8.FK_ID_SUFFIX.false_positives: A project that deliberately uses another suffix, or none — a schema inherited from a system with its own convention, or a team that passes every foreign key explicitly on purpose. Set `sqlens.audit.naming.foreign_key_suffix` to what the project actually uses, or exempt the column names through `sqlens.audit.naming.exempt`. A composite foreign key is never reported: its columns reference a compound natural key and carry their own names, so `_id` is not the convention for them.

MY.L8.NAMING_SNAKE_CASE.note: What MySQL does with a mixed-case table name is decided by `lower_case_table_names`, a SERVER setting that defaults to 2 on macOS and 0 on Linux. The same migration therefore makes one table on a developer machine and a different one in production, and the failure arrives later as "table doesn't exist". The setting cannot be changed after initialization.
MY.L8.NAMING_SNAKE_CASE.false_positives:
The rule reports any identifier outside `^[a-z][a-z0-9_]*$`, so the honest false positive is a project that CHOSE another shape and quotes consistently — a schema inherited from a system that spells things PascalCase, or a team whose convention is genuinely different. For them every finding is correct about the mechanism and wrong about the intent.

Three narrower sources are handled and are NOT false positives here: extension-owned objects, partitions deduplicated onto their parent, and the Laravel table prefix are all filtered by the catalog reader before a rule sees them, once for every rule. This rule adds no filter of its own, and the negative fixture proves the pass-through rather than re-implementing it.

The mitigation today is the level: this is level 8, so nothing reports it unless a project asks by raising `sqlens.level`. A project that wants the rule with a different shape needs the configurable pattern, which is deliberately not built yet.

On MySQL a COLUMN name is compared case-insensitively whatever `lower_case_table_names` says, so a mixed-case column is not a portability failure the way a table is. It is still reported, and that is a judgement rather than a measurement: a schema whose names follow one shape is one a reader can predict, and the same project is very often deployed on PostgreSQL too, where the column rule bites hard.

MY.L9.DOC_MISSING_COMMENT.note: Off by default, and level 9 is NOT the gate — `audit.documentation.require_table_comments` is. MySQL reports a missing comment as the EMPTY STRING rather than NULL, and — measured on 8.4.10 — puts the literal word `VIEW` into `TABLE_COMMENT` for every view, all by itself. The reader normalizes both, because a rule reading `VIEW` as documentation would report every view in every schema as documented.
MY.L9.DOC_MISSING_COMMENT.false_positives: The framework tables are exempt by default — `migrations`, `jobs`, `cache`, `sessions`, `failed_jobs`, `password_reset_tokens` and the rest. None will ever carry a comment and none should; without the exemption this rule reports double digits on a brand-new application. A column is judged by the exemption of the TABLE that owns it, so exempting `migrations` also exempts `migrations.batch`. A project's own list REPLACES the shipped one rather than adding to it, and names are matched WHOLE: a project's `job_applications` is not the framework's `jobs`. Extension-owned objects need no exemption — the catalog reader already filters them out.

MY.L9.TYPE_IMPLICIT_CAST.note: Half of what the PostgreSQL sibling reports cannot exist on MySQL: 8.4.10 refuses an integer-width mismatch outright with `ERROR 3780 … are incompatible`, signed or unsigned. So what survives into a MySQL catalog and still differs is a pair the server ACCEPTED and converts on every comparison — `timestamp` against `datetime`, measured as created without complaint. The conversion happens on a join the application runs constantly, and nothing in the schema records that it was ever intended.
MY.L9.TYPE_IMPLICIT_CAST.false_positives: A declared LENGTH difference is not a mismatch and is never reported: `varchar(50)` referencing `varchar(100)` is created by both engines, costs nothing, and is the most common shape in a real schema — the comparison is the base type. On PostgreSQL, `text` against `varchar` is also silent, because `pg_type` reports identical `typlen`, `typalign` and `typstorage` for them; `bpchar` is NOT in that group, because it pads. A foreign key whose far end could not be read reports undetermined rather than passing. The rule serves the audit suite only: a migration adding a foreign key carries the type of neither column, and the referenced table was created by a migration that is no longer pending.

MY.L9.VIEW_SELECT_STAR.note: A view's column list is fixed when the view is created. Measured on MySQL 8.4.10: over a two-column table, `information_schema.VIEWS.VIEW_DEFINITION` returns every column named and qualified — the star is already gone. Add a third column to the base table and it returns the same two, so the view silently stops describing its own source, and the view has to be replaced rather than altered.
MY.L9.VIEW_SELECT_STAR.false_positives: Three shapes of `*` are NOT reported, because none of them expands into the view's column list: `count(*)` (an argument, inside the function's parentheses), `price * quantity` (multiplication — what stands before the star decides), and a star inside a subquery such as `WHERE EXISTS (SELECT * FROM …)`. A star inside a string literal is not reported either. What the rule cannot see is a view whose DDL is assembled at runtime rather than written in the migration, and — structurally — anything at all in the audit suite, where the server has already expanded the star; that case is reported as undetermined rather than passed.

PG.L1.DROP_COLUMN.note: Dropping a column removes access to its data for every running app version that still selects it, and the deploy cannot be undone with a WHERE clause; deprecate first, drop behind the destructive opt-in.
PG.L1.DROP_COLUMN.false_positives: A column ADDED and dropped again inside the same migration on a PRE-EXISTING table is reported although it never held persistent data. The carve-out this rule has is per TABLE — a table the migration itself created — and the classifier does not model per-column lifetime, so the narrower case falls outside it. Accept it with #[SqlensIgnore] where it is real; the alternative would be a column-level history the canonical layer deliberately does not keep.

PG.L1.DROP_SCHEMA.note: DROP SCHEMA is not scoped to one object: it takes every table, view, sequence and routine in the namespace, and CASCADE also takes dependent objects OUTSIDE it. Laravel's schema builder cannot emit this, so it arrives through a hand-written DB::statement() that nothing reviews.
PG.L1.DROP_SCHEMA.false_positives: A schema this same migration created is reported like any other. CREATE SCHEMA is not captured as its own statement kind, so the migration context cannot tell a scratch namespace from a live one — the same carve-out DROP TABLE has is simply not available here. And because this is a statement-level rule, the finding names the REACH of the statement rather than the rows actually lost: an empty schema is reported with the same words as a full one.

PG.L1.DROP_TABLE.note: DROP TABLE removes the table and all its rows with no WHERE clause to undo it, and CASCADE widens the loss to every dependent object; a rename is reversible while the code is being retired.
PG.L1.DROP_TABLE.false_positives: The finding is about the statement's reach, not about what the table held: dropping an empty table, or one whose rows were already migrated elsewhere, reads identically to dropping a live one. The one exception is narrow and deliberate — a table this same migration created — so a scratch table created in an EARLIER migration of the same run is still reported. Nothing here reads row counts; a rule that did would be answering from the database rather than from the migration.

PG.L1.TRUNCATE.good:
// Delete in bounded batches instead of emptying the table under an exclusive lock:
DB::table('audit_scratch')->where('created_at', '<', now()->subDays(30))->limit(1000)->delete();
PG.L1.TRUNCATE.note: TRUNCATE takes a lock that excludes every concurrent reader and writer for its duration and cannot be undone by a forgotten WHERE clause; a batched delete keeps the table readable and is filterable.
PG.L1.TRUNCATE.false_positives: A TRUNCATE on a table that is already empty is reported exactly like one that discards a million rows — the rule reads the statement, not the table's contents. The same-migration carve-out covers a helper table this migration created and nothing wider, so a staging table from an earlier migration in the same run still fires. The lock half of the finding holds either way: ACCESS EXCLUSIVE is taken whether or not there is anything to remove.

PG.L2.CONSTRAINT_NOT_VALIDATED.bad: DB::statement('ALTER TABLE orders ADD CONSTRAINT orders_customer_id_fkey FOREIGN KEY (customer_id) REFERENCES customers (id)');
PG.L2.CONSTRAINT_NOT_VALIDATED.good:
DB::statement('ALTER TABLE orders ADD CONSTRAINT orders_customer_id_fkey FOREIGN KEY (customer_id) REFERENCES customers (id) NOT VALID');
DB::statement('ALTER TABLE orders VALIDATE CONSTRAINT orders_customer_id_fkey');
PG.L2.CONSTRAINT_NOT_VALIDATED.note: Adding a constraint without NOT VALID makes the server verify every existing row while it holds its lock; NOT VALID plus a separate VALIDATE splits that into a fast metadata change and a weaker-locking pass.
PG.L2.CONSTRAINT_NOT_VALIDATED.false_positives: On a table that is small or not yet serving traffic the validating scan costs nothing measurable, and the finding still reads like an outage warning — the rule sees the statement, never the row count. A constraint already written NOT VALID draws no finding, which is the safe form; the residual noise is therefore on tables where the safe form is not worth the second migration.

PG.L2.DROP_INDEX_NOT_CONCURRENT.note: A plain DROP INDEX takes an exclusive lock on the table for the duration of the drop; DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY releases the table to concurrent traffic instead.
PG.L2.DROP_INDEX_NOT_CONCURRENT.false_positives: A DROP INDEX names only the index, never its table, so the 'created in this same migration' carve-out that the create-index rule has cannot be applied here — dropping an index in the same migration that creates its table is reported. That shape is unusual (DROP TABLE removes the index for you), which is why the limit is accepted rather than worked around; a real instance is answered with #[SqlensIgnore].

PG.L2.INDEX_NOT_CONCURRENT.note: A plain CREATE INDEX holds a lock that blocks writes to the table while it builds; CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY builds without blocking writes, at the cost of running outside a transaction.
PG.L2.INDEX_NOT_CONCURRENT.false_positives: An index on a table that is small, or not yet receiving writes, blocks nobody for a measurable time, and the finding does not distinguish it — the rule reads the statement, not the table. The exception it does make is exact: an index on a table the SAME migration created is silent, because there are no writers to block and no rows to scan.

PG.L2.SET_NOT_NULL_SCAN.bad: DB::statement('ALTER TABLE orders ALTER COLUMN email SET NOT NULL');
PG.L2.SET_NOT_NULL_SCAN.good:
DB::statement('ALTER TABLE orders ADD CONSTRAINT orders_email_not_null CHECK (email IS NOT NULL) NOT VALID');
DB::statement('ALTER TABLE orders VALIDATE CONSTRAINT orders_email_not_null');
PG.L2.SET_NOT_NULL_SCAN.note: SET NOT NULL scans the whole table under its lock to prove no row is null; a CHECK (col IS NOT NULL) added NOT VALID and validated afterwards reaches the same guarantee without the blocking scan.
PG.L2.SET_NOT_NULL_SCAN.false_positives: On a table with few rows the proving scan is instant and the finding still names an outage. Two shapes are already silent and are NOT false positives: the column sitting on a table this migration created, and a migration that adds the matching CHECK (col IS NOT NULL) first — the safe pattern the finding recommends. ADD COLUMN … NOT NULL DEFAULT is a different statement this rule never matches at all.

PG.L2.TYPE_CHANGE_REWRITE.bad: DB::statement('ALTER TABLE orders ALTER COLUMN total_cents TYPE bigint');
PG.L2.TYPE_CHANGE_REWRITE.note: A type change that rewrites the table holds a lock while every row is rewritten; adding a new column and backfilling it in batches keeps the table available throughout.
PG.L2.TYPE_CHANGE_REWRITE.false_positives: The migration names only the TARGET type, never the source, so a target this rule knows rewrites is flagged even when the actual source makes the change free. The honesty is in the third value rather than in silence: a target the matrix does not classify comes back UNDETERMINED with its reason, not as a pass. A USING clause is decided outside the matrix and forces the finding unconditionally, which is correct for the server and can still overstate a USING that only re-labels.

PG.L3.CONCURRENTLY_IN_TRANSACTION.bad:
// This body runs in the migration's default transaction, where CONCURRENTLY is rejected:
DB::statement('CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_orders_customer_id ON orders (customer_id)');
PG.L3.CONCURRENTLY_IN_TRANSACTION.note: PostgreSQL refuses CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY inside a transaction block, and Laravel wraps a migration in one by default; the migration must opt out of the transaction for the statement to run at all.
PG.L3.CONCURRENTLY_IN_TRANSACTION.false_positives: Determinate for a captured migration, so there is little room to be wrong — the transaction context is read from the migration's own $withinTransaction rather than guessed. The case it cannot see is a transaction opened around the migration by something ELSE: a wrapper command, a test harness, or a deploy script running several migrations inside one BEGIN. There the statement still fails and this rule is silent, which is an under-report rather than a false positive.

PG.L3.MISSING_LOCK_TIMEOUT.bad: DB::statement('ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN notes text');
PG.L3.MISSING_LOCK_TIMEOUT.note: A lock-taking statement with no lock_timeout waits behind a long-running query for however long it takes, stalling all traffic to the table; a lock_timeout aborts the migration instead of the application.
PG.L3.MISSING_LOCK_TIMEOUT.false_positives: A migration whose lock_timeout is set OUTSIDE it — in the connection's own configuration, in a deploy wrapper, or by a PgBouncer default — is reported, because the rule reads the statement stream and a bound set elsewhere leaves no statement in it. It fires once per migration on the first strong-lock statement acting on a pre-existing object, so a migration that only creates tables, or only touches its own, is silent.

PG.L3.MISSING_STATEMENT_TIMEOUT.bad: DB::statement('ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN notes text');
PG.L3.MISSING_STATEMENT_TIMEOUT.note: A migration with no statement_timeout can run unbounded if a step is slower than expected; a statement_timeout caps the damage a single deploy step can do to a live database.
PG.L3.MISSING_STATEMENT_TIMEOUT.false_positives: The same blind spot as its lock_timeout sibling, and for the same reason: a statement_timeout that comes from the connection's configuration or from a deploy wrapper is invisible to a rule reading the migration's own statements. A lock_timeout alone deliberately does not satisfy it — the two bound different failures — so a migration that sets one and not the other is reported and that is the intended answer, not noise.

PG.L3.RISKY_OPS_SINGLE_TX.good:
// Put each locking operation in its own migration so its lock is taken and released alone:
DB::statement('ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN note_a text');
PG.L3.RISKY_OPS_SINGLE_TX.note: Several lock-taking operations in one transaction hold every lock until the whole transaction commits, widening the window in which traffic is blocked; one operation per migration keeps each lock short.
PG.L3.RISKY_OPS_SINGLE_TX.false_positives: It counts DISTINCT pre-existing tables locked in one transaction, so several fast ALTERs across several small tables are reported with the same words as a bundle of expensive ones — the sum being the concern, the rule does not weigh the parts. Tables the migration itself created are not counted, and neither is a migration that runs outside a transaction.

PG.L4.CHECK_ENUM_CHANGE.bad:
DB::statement('ALTER TABLE orders DROP CONSTRAINT orders_status_check');
DB::statement("ALTER TABLE orders ADD CONSTRAINT orders_status_check CHECK (status IN ('open', 'closed', 'refunded'))");
PG.L4.CHECK_ENUM_CHANGE.note: Dropping and re-adding a CHECK-based enum constraint in one step re-verifies every row under a lock and leaves no window for a rolling deploy; adding the new constraint NOT VALID and validating separately does neither.
PG.L4.CHECK_ENUM_CHANGE.false_positives: The shape it recognizes — a CHECK … IN (…) added while the same migration drops a constraint — also matches a migration that drops one CHECK and adds an unrelated one on a different column. The rule reads the pair, not the relationship between them. It is heuristic for a second reason as well: whether the value change actually breaks anything depends on application code no linter sees. An ADD with no matching DROP is a first-time enum column and is correctly silent.

PG.L4.CONSTRAINT_VALIDATION_PENDING.bad: DB::statement('ALTER TABLE orders ADD CONSTRAINT orders_customer_fk FOREIGN KEY (customer_id) REFERENCES customers (id) NOT VALID');
PG.L4.CONSTRAINT_VALIDATION_PENDING.note: NOT VALID is the right first step and this is not a complaint about it. Until VALIDATE CONSTRAINT runs, the constraint does not hold for the rows that were already there and the planner will not rely on it — silently, which is why the second step is the one that gets forgotten.
PG.L4.CONSTRAINT_VALIDATION_PENDING.false_positives: One shape, and it is a deliberate one: a project that splits NOT VALID and VALIDATE across two DEPLOYS on purpose, so the validation scan runs in a maintenance window rather than in the migration that adds the constraint. That is the recommended pattern for a large table, and the rule reports it anyway -- because from inside one migration set there is nothing that distinguishes it from a VALIDATE somebody forgot. It is what the debt ledger is for: the finding opens an entry with a date, the team acknowledges it with a reason, and the ledger stops asking while still remembering. Reporting nothing would mean a forgotten validation is indistinguishable from a planned one.

PG.L4.DROP_WITHOUT_DEPLOY_WINDOW.note: A table drop is a one-way deploy with no rollback; renaming to a pending-drop name keeps the data recoverable until a scheduled window makes the drop deliberate.
PG.L4.DROP_WITHOUT_DEPLOY_WINDOW.false_positives: It cannot prove the old application version is gone — that is code, not SQL — so a drop that IS the contract half of a properly sequenced expand/contract is reported exactly like a careless one. The finding is written as a prompt to confirm the sequence rather than as a verdict, for that reason. An object created in the same migration is silent: it never existed for a prior deploy to be using.

PG.L4.ENUM_ADD_VALUE.note: Adding an enum value cannot be reversed by down() — PostgreSQL has no ALTER TYPE ... DROP VALUE — so a rollback leaves the value behind; a CHECK-constrained text column keeps the change reversible.
PG.L4.ENUM_ADD_VALUE.false_positives: A value added to a type the SAME migration creates is silent, and that is the main carve-out. What is still reported is the irreversibility of an addition the author knows cannot be rolled back and has accepted — the rule states the property, and a migration cannot declare 'this one-way step is intended' in a way the rule reads. The in-transaction half of the finding is PostgreSQL 18's actual rule (the value cannot be USED in the transaction that adds it), not the pre-12 blanket ban.

PG.L4.ENUM_VALUE_REMOVED.bad: DB::statement("ALTER TYPE order_status RENAME VALUE 'pending' TO 'awaiting'");
PG.L4.ENUM_VALUE_REMOVED.note: Renaming or removing an enum value rewrites the meaning of data already stored under the old name and cannot be done in place safely; a CHECK-constrained column makes the set of values a reversible, reviewable change.
PG.L4.ENUM_VALUE_REMOVED.false_positives: The rebuild pattern is recognized by SHAPE — a migration that drops a type it did not create while building a new enum type — so a migration that legitimately replaces an unrelated type in the same step matches too. And the breakage it warns about depends on whether any running code still writes the removed value, which is application code the tool cannot see: heuristic on both halves, deliberately.

PG.L4.EXPAND_WITHOUT_CONTRACT.note: Adding a column and filling it from data that is already there is the expand step of an expand/contract deploy. It is correct, and it is half of a plan: until the contract step runs, the table holds two columns for one fact and nothing in the schema says which is authoritative. Nothing breaks, which is exactly why the second half is the one that gets forgotten. Drop the replaced column once every deployed reader has stopped using it.
PG.L4.EXPAND_WITHOUT_CONTRACT.false_positives: A column added for genuinely new data is not reported, because the rule requires a back-fill from the rows that already exist — that write is the evidence, not the name of the column. The reverse gap is real and deliberate: a back-fill that runs in a queued job instead of the migration is invisible, so a genuine expand/contract done that way is NOT flagged. And on the single-file fast path a contract step in another migration is out of view, so a finished sequence can read as unfinished — the same limit every run-wide question has there.

PG.L4.IDENTIFIER_LENGTH.note: Nothing here is over 63 bytes. The table is 32 characters and the two columns 25 and 24 — and the index name Laravel derives from all three is 89. PostgreSQL does not refuse it: it emits a `NOTICE` and creates the index under the first 63 bytes, and no migration runner surfaces that channel. Every later reference by the written name then fails, long after the deploy that caused it. The limit is measured in BYTES, so 32 two-byte characters are already over it while a character count would call them half.
PG.L4.IDENTIFIER_LENGTH.false_positives: An identifier that is long on purpose and stays inside the limit — the rule measures, it does not judge style, so a 60-character name is never reported. What it cannot see is a name assembled at runtime by code the migration calls: the rule reads the statement the schema builder compiled, so anything built after that point is outside its reach on both engines.

PG.L4.TYPE_NARROWING.bad: DB::statement('ALTER TABLE orders ALTER COLUMN total_cents TYPE integer');
PG.L4.TYPE_NARROWING.good:
// Widen, never narrow: a narrowing type change can fail or truncate on existing rows.
DB::statement('ALTER TABLE orders ALTER COLUMN total_cents TYPE bigint');
PG.L4.TYPE_NARROWING.note: Narrowing a column's type asks the server to fit every existing value into a smaller type, which errors or truncates on the first row that does not fit; widening is always safe for the stored data.
PG.L4.TYPE_NARROWING.false_positives: The target type is all the migration gives, so a target whose dominant real source is wider — integer, smallint, real — is flagged without knowing the source. Widening TO one of those from something narrower is reported as a narrowing, and the finding names the source-check as the thing to confirm for exactly that reason. A PARAMETRIZED narrowing such as varchar(255) → varchar(64) is deliberately not guessed at and is not reported at all.

PG.L5.COLLATION_VERSION_MISMATCH.bad:
-- refreshing FIRST, while the indexes are still sorted the old way:
ALTER DATABASE shop REFRESH COLLATION VERSION;
PG.L5.COLLATION_VERSION_MISMATCH.note: The example is the ORDER, because the order is the whole difficulty. A B-tree index on a text column stores its entries in the collation's sort order; change the collation — a glibc upgrade, a new ICU, an OS image bump — and that order changes underneath the index. Refreshing the recorded version first tells the server everything is current while the indexes are still sorted the old way: it silences PostgreSQL's own startup warning and leaves an equality lookup able to miss a row that is present. Reindex first, refresh second.
PG.L5.COLLATION_VERSION_MISMATCH.false_positives: A provider that reports no version at all is reported as undetermined rather than as clean — measured on PostgreSQL 18 on macOS, the libc provider reports none, so drift is undetectable there in principle. That is not the same as absent, and calling it a pass would be the silent green this package is built against. One side reporting and the other not is its own undetermined too: a recorded version with no current one means an OS change already happened and the evidence is gone.

PG.L5.FK_NO_INDEX.note: PostgreSQL indexes the referenced side of a foreign key and not the referencing one, so every DELETE or UPDATE on the parent scans the child table looking for rows that point at the row being changed. Laravel's constrained() creates the key and no index; the index is one line, and on a child table of any size it is the difference between a deploy and an outage.
PG.L5.FK_NO_INDEX.false_positives: An index whose leftmost columns are the key's columns already covers it, including a wider one — an index on (order_id, created_at) covers a key on (order_id). What does NOT count is a partial, expression or non-default-operator-class index: the check reports the key as uncovered and says explicitly that the table carries indexes it cannot reason about, because treating one as coverage would leave a scanning table unreported.

PG.L5.FK_NULLABLE_IN_UNIQUE.note: A unique key over (team_id, member_id) reads as "one row per pair", and under the default NULL treatment it is not enforced for any row whose member_id is NULL. Measured on PostgreSQL 18.4 and MySQL 8.4 alike: three rows sharing a team_id and carrying a NULL member_id all insert. The constraint holds for exactly the rows that never needed it. A key made entirely of foreign-key columns is a relationship, and a relationship with a missing side is not one.
PG.L5.FK_NULLABLE_IN_UNIQUE.false_positives: Cut narrow on purpose, because a nullable foreign key is usually correct. Nothing is reported unless the column sits inside a unique key of at least TWO columns whose every member is itself a foreign-key column. A single-column nullable unique key is the optional-one-to-one idiom (profile_id UNIQUE NULL, superseded_by_id UNIQUE NULL) and works precisely because NULLs are distinct; a key mixing a foreign key with a payload column is the application's own uniqueness rule and whether a NULL belongs in it is a domain question. The nullable PRIMARY KEY case the design started from is absent because it is unreachable: PostgreSQL refuses it outright and MySQL rewrites it. On PostgreSQL a key declared UNIQUE ... NULLS NOT DISTINCT holds across the NULL rows and is never reported; where that flag could not be read the answer is undetermined rather than either verdict.

PG.L5.FLOAT_MONEY.note: A binary float cannot represent 0.10 exactly, so ten of them do not add up to 1.00 — near enough that every screen shows 1.00 and every comparison against it fails. The error surfaces as one cent on a statement months after the schema decision, and whoever finds it has no way back to the column. decimal()/numeric stores the digits, so the arithmetic is the arithmetic of the invoice.
PG.L5.FLOAT_MONEY.false_positives: Nothing in a catalog says a column holds money, so the trigger is a heuristic on the NAME and says so in the finding itself. The dictionary splits terms by confidence for exactly this reason: a strong term (price, invoice_total, rechnungsbetrag) reports on its own, while a weak one (rate, value, wert, total) is ordinary language that is only sometimes money and needs a second, STRUCTURAL signal — a sibling currency column, or a cents segment in the name. A suffix of _amount is deliberately not such a signal, because amount is itself a weak term and would be vouching for itself. A project tunes both directions through sqlens.audit.money_columns.extra and .ignore.

PG.L5.MONEY_TYPE.note: PostgreSQL's money type is parsed and rendered through lc_monetary, so a dump restored onto a server with another locale reads the same characters as a different number — no error, no warning, just a different amount. It carries no currency of its own despite the name, and its scale is fixed by that same server setting rather than by the column.
PG.L5.MONEY_TYPE.false_positives: None by name: the type IS the finding, so unlike the float rule there is no heuristic and no guessing. The one real reason to keep money is a legacy schema whose reporting already depends on the server locale — an ignore-list entry records that decision where it stays visible, and the finding stays counted.

PG.L5.NO_PRIMARY_KEY.note: A table with no primary key cannot be replicated for UPDATE or DELETE: PostgreSQL answers “cannot update table … because it does not have a replica identity”, on the first write rather than when the publication is created. Row-level auditing and re-run-this-row recovery have nothing to identify a row by either.
PG.L5.NO_PRIMARY_KEY.false_positives: A UNIQUE index over columns that are all NOT NULL is a real substitute — it is exactly what REPLICA IDENTITY USING INDEX accepts — and such a table draws no finding. The bad example above is flagged even though it has a unique index, because the column is nullable: two rows holding NULL there are not equal to one another, so the index identifies nothing. Partial, expression and invalid indexes do not qualify either. A deliberately keyless log or staging table is a real case and belongs in the ignore list with its reason.

PG.L6.DEFAULT_TRANSACTION_ISOLATION_DRIF.bad:
ALTER SYSTEM SET default_transaction_isolation = 'serializable';
SELECT pg_reload_conf();
PG.L6.DEFAULT_TRANSACTION_ISOLATION_DRIF.good:
ALTER SYSTEM SET default_transaction_isolation = 'read committed';
SELECT pg_reload_conf();
PG.L6.DEFAULT_TRANSACTION_ISOLATION_DRIF.note: Raising the server default changes what every transaction does, including the ones the framework opens on its own behalf. At a higher level a transaction may fail with a serialization error instead of blocking, and that error is meant to be retried — but code written against Laravel's defaults has no reason to retry it, because at read committed it never occurs. The failure then shows up under concurrency rather than in development, which is the worst time to meet a new error class.
PG.L6.DEFAULT_TRANSACTION_ISOLATION_DRIF.false_positives: An application that deliberately runs serializable and has written the retry handling to match is the expected exception, not a defect — and that is the whole reason the finding is worded as a consequence rather than a mistake. It is the case to add to the ignore list with the reason recorded there. The check reads the server's value, never the reading session's, so a connection that raised its own level does not produce a server finding.

PG.L6.DEFAULT_TRANSACTION_READ_ONLY.bad:
ALTER SYSTEM SET default_transaction_read_only = on;
SELECT pg_reload_conf();
PG.L6.DEFAULT_TRANSACTION_READ_ONLY.good:
ALTER SYSTEM SET default_transaction_read_only = off;
SELECT pg_reload_conf();
PG.L6.DEFAULT_TRANSACTION_READ_ONLY.note: A transaction that does not say READ WRITE refuses writes outright, and the failure reads like a permissions problem without being one. The reason this is reported rather than merely noted is what it does to the rest of a run: an audit reasons about what a write would cost — which lock it takes, whether it rewrites the table — and on an instance that refuses the write before any of that, those statements stay true about the SQL and stop being true about this server.
PG.L6.DEFAULT_TRANSACTION_READ_ONLY.false_positives: A dedicated read replica, or an instance deliberately held read-only during a migration window, is the expected exception rather than a defect. It belongs on the ignore list with the reason recorded there. Only the server's value is judged: a read connection that sets the flag for its own session is doing exactly what it should, and is never reported as a server finding.

PG.L6.JSON_NOT_JSONB.note: json stores the document as text and re-parses it on every read that looks inside; jsonb parses once, on write. The difference that decides projects is indexing: a GIN index over jsonb answers containment and key-existence directly, while json has no operator class for them and every such query reads the whole table.
PG.L6.JSON_NOT_JSONB.false_positives: jsonb does not preserve the document as written — it drops insignificant whitespace, does not keep key order, and keeps only the last of duplicate keys. Where the stored bytes are evidence rather than data (a signed webhook payload whose signature covers the exact text, an audit record that must round-trip unmodified), json is the correct choice and this finding should be ignored deliberately. A column typed as a domain over json is not reported at all — the catalog shows the domain's name, not the underlying type.

PG.L6.PK_NOT_BIGINT.note: increments() gives a 4-byte auto-incrementing key that runs out at 2,147,483,647, with no warning on the way there — the first symptom is an INSERT failing on a table that has worked for years. id() gives a bigint. The fix is due exactly when it is most expensive, because widening the key rewrites the table and every index over it, under a lock, on your largest table.
PG.L6.PK_NOT_BIGINT.false_positives: A small lookup table will never approach the ceiling, and widening its key buys nothing. Ignore those deliberately rather than widening every table in the schema. Composite and non-integer keys are not reported at all: a composite key's range is the product of its parts, so "too narrow" stops being a property of one column.

PG.L6.PK_UUID_V4.note: A v4 UUID is random, so consecutive inserts land in unrelated places in the primary key's B-tree: every insert dirties a different page, the hot pages stop fitting in cache, and the index splits far more than a sequential key would. PostgreSQL 18's uuidv7() keeps the uniqueness a UUID is chosen for while sorting by creation time, so rows arrive at the end of the index the way a sequence would. This is a recommendation about write behavior on a table that grows, not a defect.
PG.L6.PK_UUID_V4.false_positives: A v7 UUID encodes the moment it was created, so a public identifier tells anybody holding it when the row was made. Where that matters the v4 key is the right choice and this finding should be ignored deliberately. A small table gains nothing from the change either — the cost this rule names only appears at volume.

PG.L6.SERIAL_NOT_IDENTITY.note: serial is a macro, not a type: it expands into a column, a sequence, a default and a dependency, and the catalog afterwards reports plain bigint. The three consequences are that the default can be dropped without a trace, the sequence carries its own USAGE grant so another role's INSERT fails at runtime, and an explicit id is accepted silently and collides later. An identity column keeps all three inside the column.
PG.L6.SERIAL_NOT_IDENTITY.false_positives: Three neighboring shapes are deliberately not reported. A hand-managed sequence several columns default from is a design, not an escaped serial — the AUTO dependency sits on the owning column, so a check asking whether the TABLE owns a sequence would report the borrowing column. A sequence owned by a column purely so it is dropped with it carries no default and is not reported. An identity column is never reported: its sequence is an INTERNAL dependency and it has no pg_attrdef row at all. A column whose default wraps nextval in a larger expression is reported as undetermined rather than either way, because an identity column cannot express that default.

PG.L6.STANDARD_CONFORMING_STRINGS_OFF.bad:
ALTER SYSTEM SET standard_conforming_strings = off;
SELECT pg_reload_conf();
PG.L6.STANDARD_CONFORMING_STRINGS_OFF.good:
ALTER SYSTEM SET standard_conforming_strings = on;
SELECT pg_reload_conf();
PG.L6.STANDARD_CONFORMING_STRINGS_OFF.note: Like the other server-baseline checks the example is configuration rather than a migration, because that is where the value lives. What it changes is the meaning of every ordinary literal that contains a backslash: with it off, a two-character sequence written as a backslash and an n becomes a newline, and a Windows path loses whatever its next letter escapes to. Nothing raises an error — the row simply holds something other than what the migration said, which means the same file applied to two servers produces two different databases.
PG.L6.STANDARD_CONFORMING_STRINGS_OFF.false_positives: The setting is session-settable, and an older tool or a legacy connection may turn it off for itself. That is not a server finding and is not reported: the check reads what the server hands a new connection, never what this one happens to be running with. A server correctly set to on must stay silent even when the audit's own session has it off.
