PG.L6.TIMESTAMP_NO_TZ.note: Laravel's timestamp() produces `timestamp without time zone`, which stores the digits it was handed and no clock to read them against. Two rows written a second apart by workers in different regions are stored an hour apart, and nothing in the column says so. timestampTz() stores the instant instead — converted to UTC on the way in and back on the way out — so a moment stays the same moment wherever it is read.
PG.L6.TIMESTAMP_NO_TZ.false_positives: A deliberately zone-less wall-clock column is a legitimate use and this rule cannot tell one apart: a branch that opens at 09:00 local opens at 09:00 everywhere, and converting that to an instant would be the bug. Business hours, recurring appointment times and similar columns should be ignored deliberately. A `date` column is not flagged at all — it carries no instant to convert.

PG.L6.TIMEZONE_NOT_UTC.note: Unlike most rules here the example is server configuration rather than a migration, because that is where the value lives — no migration can set it and no migration can be blamed for it. The application still stores the right instant either way; what moves is every boundary expression. A cast to date, a date_trunc('day', ...) or a "today" filter lands on the wrong day for the hours between local midnight and UTC midnight, and the size of that window changes twice a year with daylight saving.
PG.L6.TIMEZONE_NOT_UTC.false_positives: The reading session's own timezone is NOT the server's, and the check never reads it. TimeZone is settable per connection — PGTZ, a per-role ALTER ROLE ... SET, or a client library — so a correctly configured server audited from a connection running local time must not be reported, and a misconfigured one must still be reported when the audit's own connection happens to be UTC. Etc/UTC is accepted alongside UTC. GMT, Zulu and Universal are NOT accepted even though they resolve to the same offset: they are the same instant but a different statement, and a server set to one of them was configured by somebody who did not mean UTC.

PG.L7.DATA_CHECKSUMS_DISABLED.note: The example is the moment the decision is made, because that is the only moment it can be made cheaply: PostgreSQL 18 initializes with checksums on, and turning them off is now an explicit choice. On an existing cluster there is no in-place edit — pg_checksums --enable needs the cluster shut down cleanly, and the alternative is a new cluster and a dump/restore. That is why the finding describes the real path instead of proposing a setting to change.
PG.L7.DATA_CHECKSUMS_DISABLED.false_positives: A managed database that does not expose the value at all is reported as undetermined, never as a failure — 'we could not read it' and 'it is off' are different sentences, and only one of them justifies planning a migration. The check reads a cluster fact rather than a session value, so it is identical on a primary and its replicas and is not a separate finding on each.

PG.L7.INDEX_REDUNDANT.note: A b-tree index on (customer_id) answers nothing the index on (customer_id, placed_at) cannot: order is the fact, and the wider index serves every lookup the narrower one does. The narrow one is still maintained on every insert and on every update that touches its column, occupies its own pages in cache, and is one more relation to vacuum — for no read it serves alone.
PG.L7.INDEX_REDUNDANT.false_positives: The comparison is only made between indexes the reading already judged comparable, because a naive left-prefix test is wrong on the first real schema it meets and wrong in the direction that advises a DROP. A partial index, an expression or functional index, a non-default operator class, a prefix-length key and any method other than b-tree are each excluded with a NAMED skip, so a schema full of them is told they were not compared rather than handed a clean report. A unique index or primary key is never reported as the victim — dropping it changes what the schema ALLOWS, not what it costs — though it may still be the index that covers another. An index carrying an INCLUDE payload is never the victim either: measured, (a) INCLUDE (b) and (a) report the SAME key columns, so without that flag the rule would recommend dropping the more useful of the two.

PG.L7.INDEX_UNUSED.note: An index nobody reads is still written on every insert and on every update touching its columns, occupies its own pages in cache, and on PostgreSQL is one more relation for vacuum to walk. The read side gains nothing. The counter says how often it has been scanned; the window says whether that number means anything.
PG.L7.INDEX_UNUSED.false_positives: This rule is EXPERIMENTAL and opt-in, and the reason is not immaturity: its verdict depends on WHEN it is asked, which is a direct tension with the package's determinism promise. Three things the counter cannot see. Statistics are per INSTANCE, so an index read only on a replica looks unused on the primary. A query that runs monthly has not run yet if the window is shorter than a month, which is why the minimum window is configurable and defaults to 30 days. And a counter that was reset yesterday says nothing at all — that case is undetermined with a named reason, never a pass and never a finding. A primary key or unique index is never reported: it exists to refuse a write, and it has been doing that silently the whole time.

PG.L7.UNBATCHED_MASS_DML.note: A write with a predicate but no bound runs as one statement over every row it matches, holding row locks and keeping a transaction open for the whole of it — during which autovacuum cannot clean up behind it — while the migration blocks the deploy. The chunk SIGNAL is engine-specific even though the hazard is not: MySQL writes `LIMIT` on an `UPDATE` and PostgreSQL cannot, so the framework compiles the same call into a `ctid` subselect, and that is the shape this rule looks for.
PG.L7.UNBATCHED_MASS_DML.false_positives: This is a heuristic and says so in the finding: it can see that a statement is unbounded, never how many rows that means, and it never asks the server for a row count. On a small lookup table an unbounded write is a non-event and is still reported — which is why the rule sits at level 7, the band a project turns on when it wants estimates as well as facts. It is lenient in the other direction too: a `BETWEEN` silences it, because a key-range walk is the fix it recommends, and a `BETWEEN` on a non-key column bounds nothing. The `ctid` form is matched as a SHAPE rather than as a `LIMIT` keyword — `UPDATE … WHERE id IN (SELECT id FROM other LIMIT 10)` bounds the subquery and says nothing about the rows written, and accepting it would be a false negative.

PG.L8.FK_ID_SUFFIX.note: Laravel derives a relation's foreign key from the related model — `author_id` for a `User` — so `belongsTo(User::class)` resolves without being told anything. Name the column `author` and every relation on that side has to pass the key explicitly, in code nobody re-checks when the schema moves. The rule identifies the column from the CONSTRAINT, never from its name: a rule that looked for `_id` would find only the columns that already satisfy it.
PG.L8.FK_ID_SUFFIX.false_positives: A project that deliberately uses another suffix, or none — a schema inherited from a system with its own convention, or a team that passes every foreign key explicitly on purpose. Set `sqlens.audit.naming.foreign_key_suffix` to what the project actually uses, or exempt the column names through `sqlens.audit.naming.exempt`. A composite foreign key is never reported: its columns reference a compound natural key and carry their own names, so `_id` is not the convention for them.

PG.L8.NAMING_SNAKE_CASE.note: PostgreSQL folds an unquoted identifier to lower case, so `CREATE TABLE "Orders"` and `CREATE TABLE Orders` make two different tables and a later `SELECT * FROM Orders` reaches only the second. Name it in snake_case and the quoting question never comes up again.
PG.L8.NAMING_SNAKE_CASE.false_positives:
The rule reports any identifier outside `^[a-z][a-z0-9_]*$`, so the honest false positive is a project that CHOSE another shape and quotes consistently — a schema inherited from a system that spells things PascalCase, or a team whose convention is genuinely different. For them every finding is correct about the mechanism and wrong about the intent.

Three narrower sources are handled and are NOT false positives here: extension-owned objects, partitions deduplicated onto their parent, and the Laravel table prefix are all filtered by the catalog reader before a rule sees them, once for every rule. This rule adds no filter of its own, and the negative fixture proves the pass-through rather than re-implementing it.

The mitigation today is the level: this is level 8, so nothing reports it unless a project asks by raising `sqlens.level`. A project that wants the rule with a different shape needs the configurable pattern, which is deliberately not built yet.

On PostgreSQL the counter-argument is weakest: a quoted mixed-case identifier has to be quoted in every later reference forever, so the cost of the convention is paid continuously rather than once.

PG.L9.DOC_MISSING_COMMENT.note: Off by default, and level 9 is NOT the gate — `audit.documentation.require_table_comments` is. That second opt-in is the design: a project that raised its level to see the pedantic band asked for opinionated findings, not to be told in the same breath that every table it owns is undocumented. The table and column switches are separate because they are different amounts of work. PostgreSQL reports a missing comment as NULL from `obj_description` and `col_description`, measured on 18.4.
PG.L9.DOC_MISSING_COMMENT.false_positives: The framework tables are exempt by default — `migrations`, `jobs`, `cache`, `sessions`, `failed_jobs`, `password_reset_tokens` and the rest. None will ever carry a comment and none should; without the exemption this rule reports double digits on a brand-new application. A column is judged by the exemption of the TABLE that owns it, so exempting `migrations` also exempts `migrations.batch`. A project's own list REPLACES the shipped one rather than adding to it, and names are matched WHOLE: a project's `job_applications` is not the framework's `jobs`. Extension-owned objects need no exemption — the catalog reader already filters them out.

PG.L9.TYPE_IMPLICIT_CAST.note: The usual reason given for this — "the comparison stops using the index" — was measured against PostgreSQL 18.4 and is FALSE: `EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM invoices WHERE account_id = 42::bigint` answers `Index Scan … Index Cond: (account_id = '42'::bigint)`, because the btree integer operator family carries cross-type operators. What is actually wrong is worse and it is dated: an `int` column can only ever point at the first 2,147,483,647 of a `bigint` key's values. Every test passes, because a test database never gets there — and then the parent sequence crosses that number, years later, and every insert into the child fails.
PG.L9.TYPE_IMPLICIT_CAST.false_positives: A declared LENGTH difference is not a mismatch and is never reported: `varchar(50)` referencing `varchar(100)` is created by both engines, costs nothing, and is the most common shape in a real schema — the comparison is the base type. On PostgreSQL, `text` against `varchar` is also silent, because `pg_type` reports identical `typlen`, `typalign` and `typstorage` for them; `bpchar` is NOT in that group, because it pads. A foreign key whose far end could not be read reports undetermined rather than passing. The rule serves the audit suite only: a migration adding a foreign key carries the type of neither column, and the referenced table was created by a migration that is no longer pending.

PG.L9.VIEW_SELECT_STAR.note: A view's column list is fixed when the view is created. Measured on PostgreSQL 18.4: over a two-column table, `pg_get_viewdef` returns `SELECT a, b FROM t` — the star is already gone. Add a third column to the base table and it returns the same two, so the view silently stops describing its own source. Nothing about the `ALTER TABLE` says so, and the report that quietly lacks the new column is noticed weeks later by somebody who does not know a view is involved.
PG.L9.VIEW_SELECT_STAR.false_positives: Three shapes of `*` are NOT reported, because none of them expands into the view's column list: `count(*)` (an argument, inside the function's parentheses), `price * quantity` (multiplication — what stands before the star decides), and a star inside a subquery such as `WHERE EXISTS (SELECT * FROM …)`. A star inside a string literal is not reported either. What the rule cannot see is a view whose DDL is assembled at runtime rather than written in the migration, and — structurally — anything at all in the audit suite, where the server has already expanded the star; that case is reported as undetermined rather than passed.

SEC.AUTH.HBA_CLEARTEXT.note: The password method sends the password itself — not hashed, not challenged. On a hostnossl line the connection is never encrypted and the credential is readable by anything on the path; on a hostssl line TLS protects it in transit, which makes it a weak method rather than an exposed credential. Change the method to scram-sha-256: every supported client library speaks it, and it never puts the password on the wire.
SEC.AUTH.HBA_CLEARTEXT.false_positives: A plain host line may or may not negotiate TLS depending on the client and on ssl on the server, and this check does not read that setting — the finding says so rather than guessing. SEC.AUTH.HBA_OPEN_CIDR is what tells you how wide the exposure is.

SEC.AUTH.HBA_MD5.note: md5 has been superseded since PostgreSQL 10 and is deprecated: the role name is the only salt, so a captured digest is both crackable offline and usable AS the password. Change it in this order or the roles will be unable to authenticate — set password_encryption to scram-sha-256, have each role set its password again so a SCRAM verifier is stored, and only then change the line. What each role currently has stored is a separate finding.
SEC.AUTH.HBA_MD5.false_positives: A client library too old to speak SCRAM is the only real constraint, and it is worth measuring rather than assuming — the drivers that could not have all been able to for years.

SEC.AUTH.HBA_OPEN_CIDR.good:
hostssl all    app    10.0.4.0/24  scram-sha-256
hostssl all    app    2001:db8:4::/64  scram-sha-256
SEC.AUTH.HBA_OPEN_CIDR.note: The line matches every address there is, so the server offers authentication to any host that can route to it. A correct method still asks for a credential — but it asks EVERYONE, which turns every password into the only thing between the internet and this database. Narrow the line to the networks that actually connect, and let everything else be refused before a password is ever guessed at.
SEC.AUTH.HBA_OPEN_CIDR.false_positives: A cluster that is genuinely only reachable through a private network — a managed provider terminating connections at its own proxy — is where an open range is a considered choice. The finding names the method on the line too, because 0.0.0.0/0 with trust or with md5 is a different order of problem than 0.0.0.0/0 with SCRAM.

SEC.AUTH.HBA_PARSE_ERROR.note: PostgreSQL reports the line as having an error and SKIPS it — the server starts, the file loads, and the restriction the line was written to impose is not in force. The next matching line decides who connects instead, which is usually a broader one. Fix the line, reload the configuration with SELECT pg_reload_conf(), then re-read pg_hba_file_rules to confirm the error is gone.
SEC.AUTH.HBA_PARSE_ERROR.false_positives: The same rule reports a second, rarer shape: pg_hba_file_rules answering without refusing and returning no rules at all. That cannot describe a live server — one with no host-based authentication rules accepts no connections, and the audit arrived over one — so it is reported as nothing having been checked rather than as a clean result.

SEC.AUTH.HBA_TRUST.bad:
# pg_hba.conf — any host on the network can be any role
host    all    all    0.0.0.0/0    trust
SEC.AUTH.HBA_TRUST.good:
# a method that authenticates, and a range that is actually used
hostssl all    app    10.0.4.0/24  scram-sha-256
SEC.AUTH.HBA_TRUST.note: trust on a network line means no credential is asked for at all: anyone who can reach this server and name a role IS that role. Passwords stored for those roles are not consulted, so rotating them changes nothing. Replace trust with scram-sha-256 on the line, and narrow the address range if it does not need to be that wide.
SEC.AUTH.HBA_TRUST.false_positives: None worth calling one. A test cluster on a loopback-only listener is the closest case, and even there the line is one listen_addresses change away from being reachable — which is why this rule is the only critical in the HBA family.

SEC.AUTH.HBA_TRUST_LOCAL.good:
# the operator account authenticates as the OS user it already is
local   all    postgres    peer

# the application presents a password like any other client
local   all    app         scram-sha-256
SEC.AUTH.HBA_TRUST_LOCAL.note: trust on a local line is narrower than the same setting on a network line (SEC.AUTH.HBA_TRUST) — the Unix socket has to be reachable first — and it still means OS access and database access are the same thing here: any process that can open the socket connects as any role it names, including roles it was never granted. Use peer for the operator account and scram-sha-256 for the application.
SEC.AUTH.HBA_TRUST_LOCAL.false_positives: A single-user development machine is the usual reason this line exists, and on one it is a considered choice rather than a defect. It is reported at medium rather than critical for exactly that reason.

SEC.AUTH.PASSWORD_LITERAL_IN_MIGRATION.note: A literal puts the credential in version control — in every clone, in the reflog after somebody removes it in a later commit, and in any CI log that echoed the migration. Rotating it then means rotating it everywhere it was copied to, and nobody knows where that is. Supply it through a binding or an environment read so the value never becomes part of the statement. The finding deliberately shows neither the value nor the statement: a finding travels into a JSON report, a SARIF file and a committed agent artifact, and quoting the secret would republish it further than the migration did.
SEC.AUTH.PASSWORD_LITERAL_IN_MIGRATION.false_positives: The rule cannot tell a real credential from a throwaway one, so a migration that sets a password for a role it drops three statements later is reported the same way. It is PATH-BOUND: the identical statement in a seeder or a factory is silent, because that is test data and a rule wrong on the majority of a repository's literals gets switched off entirely. Where the origin cannot be established — a snippet passed to --file — the answer is undetermined with the reason named, never a pass and never a Critical on suspicion.

SEC.AUTH.ROLE_ANONYMOUS.note: The empty user name is the part that misreads: it looks like an account nobody uses, and it is an account anybody can use. A client connecting from a matching host under a name the server does not know is authenticated as this one, with whatever privileges it holds — so every typo and every stale credential from that host lands here instead of being refused. It does have a password, which is the only thing separating it from the critical case.
SEC.AUTH.ROLE_ANONYMOUS.false_positives: Close to none on a server installed this decade: MySQL stopped shipping anonymous accounts long ago and mysql_secure_installation removes them. A hit is almost always an account carried through upgrades from a much older server — which is precisely the account nobody remembers creating. If something does depend on it, that dependency is worth writing down before it is removed.

SEC.AUTH.ROLE_ANONYMOUS_NO_PASSWORD.bad:
-- No name required, and no password either.
CREATE USER ''@'localhost';
SEC.AUTH.ROLE_ANONYMOUS_NO_PASSWORD.good:
-- There is no configuration that makes this safe. Remove it.
DROP USER ''@'localhost';
SEC.AUTH.ROLE_ANONYMOUS_NO_PASSWORD.note: The two worst account states at once, and the shortest way into a server that exists. The empty name means a client picks whatever name it likes; the empty credential means nothing is then asked of it. Reported as ONE finding rather than as an anonymous finding plus a no-password finding — it is one account and one fact, and two ids would read as two problems.
SEC.AUTH.ROLE_ANONYMOUS_NO_PASSWORD.false_positives: None worth naming. Unlike the anonymous-with-password case there is no arrangement in which this is deliberate, and unlike the plain no-password case there is no external authenticator to consider — an anonymous account is a password-plugin account by construction.

SEC.AUTH.ROLE_DEPRECATED_PASSWORD_HASH.bad:
-- MySQL: the plugin 9.0 removes
ALTER USER 'app'@'%' IDENTIFIED WITH mysql_native_password BY 'secret';
SEC.AUTH.ROLE_DEPRECATED_PASSWORD_HASH.good:
-- MySQL: current verifier, and one that still exists after the next major
ALTER USER 'app'@'%' IDENTIFIED WITH caching_sha2_password BY 'secret';
SEC.AUTH.ROLE_DEPRECATED_PASSWORD_HASH.note: The account can log in right now, and the verifier protecting it is the weaker one its engine offers. On MySQL there is a second, separate problem arriving with it: mysql_native_password is off by default in 8.4 and REMOVED in 9.0, so the account stops being able to log in at the next major — during an upgrade window, with nothing in the connection string to warn anybody. On PostgreSQL the md5 verifier is salted with the ROLE NAME and nothing else, so a captured digest is crackable offline and usable as the password itself against any server where a role of that name exists.
SEC.AUTH.ROLE_DEPRECATED_PASSWORD_HASH.false_positives: None measured on a stock server: all six accounts on a fresh MySQL 8.4, including the three mysql.* system ones, are caching_sha2_password. A deprecated verifier is nobody's default, which is why this rule reports every non-system account rather than only the one the audit connected as. A client library too old to speak the newer handshake is the one real constraint, and it is worth measuring rather than assuming.

SEC.AUTH.ROLE_DEPRECATED_PASSWORD_HASH_L.note: Reported at low rather than skipped, and the distinction is the whole point: locking an account is not fixing it. Unlocking is one statement, and the account comes back carrying exactly the verifier it went away with. A rule that stayed silent here would make ACCOUNT LOCK look like a remediation.
SEC.AUTH.ROLE_DEPRECATED_PASSWORD_HASH_L.false_positives: A deliberately retired account nobody intends to unlock is the expected case, and it belongs on the ignore list with that reason written down — which is a better record than silence, because the next person to consider unlocking it can read it.

SEC.AUTH.ROLE_NO_PASSWORD.note: The account can log in and there is no password to get past. Anyone who reaches the port and knows the name is already in — nothing to crack, capture or intercept, which makes this the shortest path into a database there is. The fix is one statement either way, and which one depends on a decision rather than on a technique: is this account supposed to authenticate with a password, or with something the database does not hold?
SEC.AUTH.ROLE_NO_PASSWORD.false_positives: The one shape that looks like this and is not: an account whose credential genuinely lives outside the database — auth_socket, PAM, LDAP — has an empty credential field by design. The reading draws that line from the PLUGIN rather than from the empty field, so those accounts never reach this rule. A check written against the column instead would report every socket-authenticated account on every server. PostgreSQL is excluded for a related reason: there a role without a password is ordinary and frequently correct, and whether anyone can connect as it is decided in pg_hba.conf, which SEC.AUTH.HBA_TRUST reads.

SEC.AUTH.ROLE_NO_PASSWORD_LOCKED.note: The lock is the only thing in the way. ALTER USER … ACCOUNT UNLOCK removes it in one statement, and what comes back is an account anyone who knows its name can log into. Reported at low rather than skipped for exactly that reason: locking an account is not the same as giving it a password, and a report that stayed silent here would let the lock read as a fix.
SEC.AUTH.ROLE_NO_PASSWORD_LOCKED.false_positives: An account deliberately parked and about to be dropped will show up here, which is the intended behavior rather than a miss: dropping it is one of the two suggested fixes. As with the usable case, an account whose credential lives outside the database is never reported — the reading classifies it by plugin, not by an empty field.

SEC.AUTH.ROLE_WILDCARD_HOST.bad:
-- Reachable from every address the server has.
CREATE USER 'deploy'@'%' IDENTIFIED BY 'a real secret';
SEC.AUTH.ROLE_WILDCARD_HOST.good:
-- Reachable from the network the client actually comes from.
CREATE USER 'deploy'@'10.0.0.%' IDENTIFIED BY 'a real secret';
SEC.AUTH.ROLE_WILDCARD_HOST.note: The host half of a MySQL account name is an access control, not a label: `%` matches every address the server can be reached at. On an account with ordinary privileges this is a pattern worth tightening rather than an emergency, which is why it is medium — the finding is the list of accounts for which that decision should have been made on purpose.
SEC.AUTH.ROLE_WILDCARD_HOST.false_positives: A wildcard host is the correct choice for some accounts. Replication and monitoring reach a server from addresses nobody wants to enumerate, and a container platform can reassign a client's address on every deploy. The finding says so rather than assuming otherwise; what it gives you is the list, not a verdict on each entry.

SEC.AUTH.ROLE_WILDCARD_HOST_PRIVILEGED.note: Neither half is remarkable alone — plenty of accounts are reachable from anywhere for good reasons, and every server has privileged accounts. Together they leave nothing between the whole network and an account with nothing above it to escalate to: one leaked or guessed credential is the entire attack. The two fixes are independent, so doing either one is already progress.
SEC.AUTH.ROLE_WILDCARD_HOST_PRIVILEGED.false_positives: Fewer than for the medium case, and that is the point of separating them: an account that genuinely needs both is rare enough to be worth naming in a comment beside the GRANT. Where the privileges really are required, narrow the host — it is the half nobody has to reason about at run time.

SEC.CFG.GENERAL_LOG.bad:
# my.cnf: every statement written down, verbatim and unredacted.
general_log = ON
SEC.CFG.GENERAL_LOG.good:
# Off is the vendor default, and where a server should be between debugging sessions.
general_log = OFF
SEC.CFG.GENERAL_LOG.note: The log does not redact, because it is a debugging tool: it records what was sent. CREATE USER ... IDENTIFIED BY goes in with the password, and so does any value interpolated into SQL rather than bound. MySQL does rewrite passwords before logging -- in the ERROR log and the slow log, not here -- which is why a reader who has heard that MySQL redacts has heard something true about a different log.
SEC.CFG.GENERAL_LOG.false_positives: A server with it deliberately on while somebody is debugging is the legitimate case, and it is measured in minutes. Nothing here can tell that apart from a switch somebody forgot, which is the point: the cost is silent and grows with uptime. What this cannot see is where the log goes or who can read it -- those are questions about the host, not the catalog.

SEC.CFG.GENERAL_LOG_PERSONAL_DATA.bad:
# my.cnf: every statement written down, verbatim — values included.
general_log = ON
SEC.CFG.GENERAL_LOG_PERSONAL_DATA.good:
# Off is the vendor default, and where a production server belongs.
general_log = OFF
SEC.CFG.GENERAL_LOG_PERSONAL_DATA.note: The privacy half of the same switch its hardening sibling SEC.CFG.GENERAL_LOG reads. That one is about secrets — a password in a CREATE USER goes into the log. This one is about the rows: every WHERE email = ... with its value, every name and address an INSERT carries. The two are gated by different categories and usually read by different people, which is why one rule cannot serve both: a report missing a category looks exactly like a clean report.
SEC.CFG.GENERAL_LOG_PERSONAL_DATA.false_positives: A server with the log deliberately on while somebody debugs, which is measured in minutes. This rule reports only on production, so a laptop or a staging box that the run can place is silent; where it cannot place the environment it answers undetermined rather than guessing.

SEC.CFG.LOCAL_INFILE.bad:
# my.cnf: the server may ask the client to send it a file.
local_infile = ON
SEC.CFG.LOCAL_INFILE.good:
# Off is the vendor default on 8.4, and costs an application nothing.
local_infile = OFF
SEC.CFG.LOCAL_INFILE.note: The direction is the opposite of what the statement name suggests. LOAD DATA LOCAL INFILE does not read a file on the server: the server names a path and the CLIENT reads it off its own disk and uploads it, so a compromised server can ask an application for its .env without the application running any LOAD DATA of its own. No privilege on the account is involved — the capability is negotiated at connection time, not granted.
SEC.CFG.LOCAL_INFILE.false_positives: A data-import job that genuinely uses LOAD DATA LOCAL INFILE is the case worth checking before turning it off; it can be enabled for the one session that needs it. Note also that this reads the SERVER's side of the negotiation only: current PHP builds refuse the transfer client-side by default, which this rule cannot see and does not claim to.

SEC.CFG.LOCAL_INFILE_FILE_GRANT.bad:
# my.cnf: the server would ask a client for a file...
local_infile = ON

# ...and an account here can also write one on the server's own disk:
#   GRANT FILE ON *.* TO 'reporting'@'%';
SEC.CFG.LOCAL_INFILE_FILE_GRANT.note: Reported BESIDE SEC.CFG.LOCAL_INFILE rather than instead of it, because the two say different sentences: that one is about the server's capability, this one about what exists on this instance alongside it. Severity is metadata on the rule here, so an escalation is a second id -- and the deduplication key is rule id AND location, so both survive into one report.
SEC.CFG.LOCAL_INFILE_FILE_GRANT.false_positives: The escalation is only made when the grant tables were actually READABLE. On a managed MySQL a refused grant read is the ordinary case, and there the run reports that it could not check rather than quietly declining to escalate -- a silent non-escalation is indistinguishable from one that correctly found no such account.

SEC.CFG.PASSWORD_ENCRYPTION.bad:
# postgresql.conf: every password set from now on is stored as an md5 verifier.
password_encryption = md5
SEC.CFG.PASSWORD_ENCRYPTION.good:
# The default since PostgreSQL 14. A configuration reload picks this up; no restart.
password_encryption = scram-sha-256
SEC.CFG.PASSWORD_ENCRYPTION.note: The only finding in the md5 family that reports a server which is clean today -- its siblings need an account or an authentication rule that already carries the weak hash, this one needs neither. It is about the NEXT password: nothing fails, nothing warns at the connection, and every ALTER ROLE ... PASSWORD from here on quietly produces a verifier salted with the ROLE NAME and nothing else, which makes the same password under the same role name the same digest on every server that carries it.
SEC.CFG.PASSWORD_ENCRYPTION.false_positives: Existing passwords are untouched by a fix here, so a server that passes this check may still be full of md5 verifiers -- those are reported per account, by a different rule. And the parameter has context user: any session may set it for itself, so the server's value is the default new connections inherit rather than a rule they cannot break. Fixing it stops the server producing md5 verifiers by default; it does not make them impossible.

SEC.CFG.PATCH_EOL.bad:
-- What the server answers, and what the rule reads.
SHOW server_version;   -- 13.22
-- PostgreSQL 13 left support on 2025-11-13: no further minor release
-- will ever carry a fix for it.
SEC.CFG.PATCH_EOL.good:
-- The same question on a series still inside its window.
SHOW server_version;   -- 18.4
-- PostgreSQL 18 is supported until 2030-11-14.
SEC.CFG.PATCH_EOL.note: There is no SQL that fixes this, which is unusual for a finding and worth saying plainly: the remediation is a major upgrade, planned and scheduled, and no setting substitutes for it. The examples show the READING rather than a repair because that is the entire surface a database exposes here -- the rule judges what the instance says it is.
SEC.CFG.PATCH_EOL.false_positives: A vendor-patched build that carries security fixes past the upstream date reads as out of support here, because the version string is all a server offers and it does not distinguish a distribution's backports from upstream's own releases. That is the honest limit of an offline check: the alternative would be trusting a build suffix, which anybody can set. Such a server is suppressed through the baseline once, with the reason recorded.

SEC.CFG.REQUIRE_SECURE_TRANSPORT.bad:
# my.cnf: a connection that skips encryption is accepted like any other.
require_secure_transport = OFF
SEC.CFG.REQUIRE_SECURE_TRANSPORT.good:
# Refuse anything that did not negotiate a secure transport.
require_secure_transport = ON
SEC.CFG.REQUIRE_SECURE_TRANSPORT.note: This is not "encryption is off". MySQL 8 negotiates TLS by default and most clients take it, so a server with this OFF usually looks encrypted from the inside -- every connection somebody checks is one that happened to negotiate it. What the setting decides is whether one that did NOT is refused, and a client that omits TLS or whose setup silently failed connects exactly as before, in the clear, with nothing raised anywhere.
SEC.CFG.REQUIRE_SECURE_TRANSPORT.false_positives: Several managed providers enforce transport at a proxy OUTSIDE the server configuration; the variable then reads OFF on a server no connection can reach in the clear. The finding says the SERVER does not require it and says so in those words. A deployment on a private network is the other case worth weighing -- the exposure is bounded by that network, which is why this is reported below the findings that need nothing else to be true.

SEC.CFG.SECURE_FILE_PRIV.bad:
# my.cnf: no limit at all on where FILE may read and write.
# (MySQL reports this state as the EMPTY value.)
secure_file_priv =
SEC.CFG.SECURE_FILE_PRIV.good:
# Switch the operations off entirely. MySQL reports this as the string NULL.
secure_file_priv = NULL

# …or confine them to one directory, if an import job genuinely needs them.
secure_file_priv = /var/lib/mysql-files
SEC.CFG.SECURE_FILE_PRIV.note: The empty value is the dangerous one, and that is the opposite of what it looks like. MySQL writes the switched-off state as the string NULL, so the server that appears unconfigured is the one with no limit, and the server that appears to have some value set is the hardened one. Reported at high rather than critical because on its own it grants nobody anything: it is the multiplier on the FILE privilege, not a privilege.
SEC.CFG.SECURE_FILE_PRIV.false_positives: A directory is a deliberate limit and is never reported. So is the disabled state. The only finding is the empty value, which means this rule is silent on every server somebody has actually configured — a data-import job that uses LOAD DATA INFILE keeps working with a directory set.

SEC.CFG.STATEMENT_LOGGING.bad:
# postgresql.conf: every statement and every parameter value, written to the server log.
log_statement = all
SEC.CFG.STATEMENT_LOGGING.good:
# Schema statements carry column names, never row values — an audit trail without the data.
log_statement = ddl
SEC.CFG.STATEMENT_LOGGING.note: The only rule in the pack whose verdict depends on something outside the database: the same value is how people debug on a laptop. On a production instance `all` writes every `WHERE email = '...'` into a text file that is routinely read by operators who were never granted the table, shipped to an aggregator under its own retention, and kept in backups that outlive the row an erasure request removed. `mod` is narrower and still reaches data — every row a migration or a job writes, verbatim. `ddl` is where the line falls: schema statements name columns, not people.
SEC.CFG.STATEMENT_LOGGING.false_positives: A server deliberately logging everything while somebody debugs a production incident is the legitimate case, and nothing here can tell it from a switch left on afterwards. The environment condition is the other half: when nothing places the run as production — `app.env` unset or a name this check does not recognize — the answer is `undetermined` rather than a pass, because reporting a pass would state something about a server nobody placed.

SEC.CFG.STATEMENT_LOGGING_SECRETS.bad:
# postgresql.conf: every statement, and every value in it, into the log.
log_statement = 'all'
SEC.CFG.STATEMENT_LOGGING_SECRETS.good:
# Schema changes keep an audit trail; row values never reach the log.
log_statement = 'ddl'
SEC.CFG.STATEMENT_LOGGING_SECRETS.note: The hardening half of the switch its privacy sibling SEC.CFG.STATEMENT_LOGGING reads, and the half that was missing until 2026-08-13: MySQL had a secrets view of general_log and PostgreSQL only a privacy view of log_statement, so a team filtering on --category=security never saw that CREATE ROLE ... LOGIN PASSWORD writes the password into the log. Nothing was red; the report simply had no finding in it.
SEC.CFG.STATEMENT_LOGGING_SECRETS.false_positives: mod rather than all narrows it to writes, which is a real mitigation and still logs every value a migration or job writes. ddl and none carry no values and are not reported. A short debugging window is legitimate and indistinguishable from a forgotten switch, which is the point: the cost is silent and grows with uptime.

SEC.CFG.TLS_DISABLED.bad:
# postgresql.conf: the server cannot negotiate TLS at all.
ssl = off
SEC.CFG.TLS_DISABLED.good:
# Offer TLS. A configuration reload picks this up; no restart.
ssl = on
ssl_cert_file = /etc/ssl/certs/server.crt
ssl_key_file = /etc/ssl/private/server.key
SEC.CFG.TLS_DISABLED.note: Stronger than an unenforced transport, and the difference matters when deciding what to fix first. A server that offers TLS without insisting on it still encrypts most connections; a server with ssl off encrypts none, including the ones somebody checks. And no client can make up for it: insisting on TLS against such a server fails the connection rather than securing it.
SEC.CFG.TLS_DISABLED.false_positives: A database reached only over a unix socket, or over a private network it shares with nothing else, is bounded by that network rather than by this setting -- which is why this is reported below critical. A managed provider that terminates TLS at a proxy is the other case: the server parameter reads off while no connection reaches it in the clear.

SEC.CFG.TLS_MIN_VERSION.bad:
# postgresql.conf: TLS is on, and TLS 1.0 is still on the table.
ssl = on
ssl_min_protocol_version = 'TLSv1'
SEC.CFG.TLS_MIN_VERSION.good:
# The vendor default, and the floor this rule checks against.
ssl = on
ssl_min_protocol_version = 'TLSv1.2'
SEC.CFG.TLS_MIN_VERSION.note: Harder to notice than TLS being off, because nothing looks wrong: every connection reports as encrypted and a dashboard says so. What the low minimum adds is a version an active attacker on the path can negotiate down to. The default has been TLSv1.2 for as long as the parameter has existed, so a server below it was moved there deliberately -- usually years ago, for one client that no longer connects.
SEC.CFG.TLS_MIN_VERSION.false_positives: A deployment whose clients all insist on TLS 1.3 is never exposed to the older version this reports, and nothing about the clients is visible from the catalog. A managed provider that terminates or re-negotiates TLS at a proxy is the other case: the parameter reads the same whether or not anything can reach it.

SEC.INJ.DYNAMIC_IDENTIFIER.note: A column name is part of the statement's grammar, so there is no placeholder to bind it to and no escaping that makes it safe. The answer is an allowlist — compare the input against columns you wrote, then pass one of those — and the rule already recognizes the three shapes teams write for it: a guard like this one, a constant map, and a match over constants.
SEC.INJ.DYNAMIC_IDENTIFIER.false_positives: Sorting is the most common thing a listing page does, so the rule is deliberately narrow: it fires only where the column is BOTH unknown at analysis time AND visibly from the request. A column that arrives through a validated form request is still unknown to the analyzer and is reported, although the validation has already reduced it to the allowlist.

SEC.INJ.RAW_INTERPOLATION.note: The interpolated value ends up inside the statement text, so whatever it contains is read as SQL grammar rather than as data. Moving it into a bindings array is the whole fix wherever one exists — a bound value cannot change what the statement does. Two cases have none: DB::raw() and DB::unprepared() take no bindings parameter at all, and an identifier or DDL position accepts no placeholder in any engine. There the exemption belongs in PHPStan's ignoreErrors, keyed on this rule's identifier and scoped to a path; analyse.exclude_paths governs the justification duty and deliberately does not reach this rule.
SEC.INJ.RAW_INTERPOLATION.false_positives: A fragment assembled only from constants is still entirely the author's, so 'ANALYZE '.self::TABLE is not reported, and neither is a lookup into a constant map — the shape a team already writes as an allowlist. Where the rule does cry wolf is a value reaching the call site through a helper the analyzer cannot follow: it is reported as interpolated even when that helper only ever returns one of a handful of literals. The other standing case is not a false positive but an unactionable one: an interpolated identifier, schema name or enum-built CHECK constraint is correctly reported and cannot be rewritten, because no engine binds a parameter in those positions.

SEC.INJ.RAW_SQL_WITHOUT_REASON.note: The rule reports raw SQL carrying no written reason, not raw SQL as such. The attribute takes that reason, nothing parses it, and it exists for the next reader. Prefer it on the method: a class-level reason covers every raw call in the class, so one careless call is excused by one considered one — silently.
SEC.INJ.RAW_SQL_WITHOUT_REASON.false_positives: A raw call whose justification sits in a comment above it is still reported, although the reasoning a reader needs is right there. The rule reads the attribute only, because a comment cannot be found by tooling and a requirement nothing can check is not a requirement.

SEC.PII.UNENCRYPTED_COLUMN.note: The pair is a MODEL rather than a migration, and that is the point: nothing about the column changes. The database sees the same varchar either way, and what decides whether the value is readable is one line of application code. That is also why this rule needs the application's models at all -- a catalog reading alone cannot answer it.
SEC.PII.UNENCRYPTED_COLUMN.false_positives: Two shapes, both expected, and the reason both severities sit below the gate default. A column whose NAME suggests personal data and whose contents are a label, a reference or an enum: add it to sqlens.security.privacy.ignore_columns. And a column encrypted by something other than an Eloquent cast, such as an application-level envelope or a column key in the database -- this rule cannot see either, so the finding is still the right question and the ignore list is the right answer to it.

SEC.PRIV.CONNECTIONS_UNSEPARATED.note: One connection for requests and migrations means the role that serves a request holds whatever DDL the migrations need. A SQL injection reaching that connection can then change the schema rather than only the rows, and a table, function or trigger it leaves behind outlives the request that created it. Splitting the connections is a config change, not a schema change: the runtime role keeps DML, the migration role keeps the DDL rights.
SEC.PRIV.CONNECTIONS_UNSEPARATED.false_positives: A project that deliberately deploys as the runtime role — a single-developer app, a throwaway environment — is the expected exception, and the ignore entry should record that. The rule reads the configured connections, not the privileges themselves: SEC.PRIV.RUNTIME_DDL is the finding that reads what the role actually holds.

SEC.PRIV.GRANT_ADMIN_IN_MIGRATION.good: DB::statement("GRANT SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE ON app.orders TO 'app_runtime'@'localhost'");
SEC.PRIV.GRANT_ADMIN_IN_MIGRATION.note: SELECT on a table is a question about rows. FILE, PROCESS, RELOAD, SHUTDOWN, CREATE USER and the dynamic privileges that replaced SUPER are questions about the SERVER: reading and writing files as the server process, seeing every session's statements, flushing the grant tables, stopping the server, minting another account. An application account needs none of them, and a migration is where one quietly acquires them.
SEC.PRIV.GRANT_ADMIN_IN_MIGRATION.false_positives: A backup, replication or operations account legitimately needs several of these, and the statement does not say which kind of account it is addressing. The safe form is not a narrower version of the same privilege — there is no narrower FILE — but a separate account for the operational job. PostgreSQL is never reported: its administrative rights are role ATTRIBUTES set by CREATE ROLE / ALTER ROLE, not privileges handed out by GRANT.

SEC.PRIV.GRANT_ALL.note: There is no privilege escalation left to perform against an account in this state — anything that reaches the connection already has everything, so every narrower finding in this suite describes a step somebody no longer has to take. The words ALL PRIVILEGES are not what is detected: both engines expand them at grant time, so the state is recognized by comparing what the account holds against what the engine has for that kind of object.
SEC.PRIV.GRANT_ALL.false_positives: Administrative, replication and migration accounts are deliberately broad, and the finding does not claim any single entry is wrong. It is the LIST of accounts for which this ought to have been a decision — its value is a name on it that nobody expected. Grants the ENGINE ships are never reported at all, so a server's own internal accounts stay out of it.

SEC.PRIV.GRANT_EXCESSIVE_IN_MIGRATION.bad: DB::statement('GRANT ALL PRIVILEGES ON orders TO app_runtime');
SEC.PRIV.GRANT_EXCESSIVE_IN_MIGRATION.good: DB::statement('GRANT SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE ON orders TO app_runtime');
SEC.PRIV.GRANT_EXCESSIVE_IN_MIGRATION.note: ALL PRIVILEGES is the shape somebody reaches for while getting a migration to run, and it is invisible afterwards: read out of the catalog it looks like a decision. WITH GRANT OPTION is smaller on the page and larger in effect — it does not widen what this role may do, it lets the role widen what everyone else may do, so the privilege set stops being something the migration history describes. Grant the privileges the role actually uses, by name.
SEC.PRIV.GRANT_EXCESSIVE_IN_MIGRATION.false_positives: A migration's OWNER role legitimately holds a great deal, and an extension's install script grants broadly by design. Neither is distinguishable from an over-grant by reading the statement — the difference is in what the role is for. A grant whose target is PUBLIC is NOT reported here: SEC.PRIV.GRANT_PUBLIC_IN_MIGRATION owns that statement whole, so the two rules never both speak for one line.

SEC.PRIV.GRANT_FILE.bad:
-- Reads and writes files as the SERVER's operating-system user.
GRANT FILE ON *.* TO 'app'@'10.0.0.%';
SEC.PRIV.GRANT_FILE.good:
-- An application account has no use for it.
REVOKE FILE ON *.* FROM 'app'@'10.0.0.%';

-- And on the server, confine what FILE can reach at all:
-- secure_file_priv = /var/lib/mysql-files   (a directory)
-- secure_file_priv = NULL                    (disabled entirely)
SEC.PRIV.GRANT_FILE.note: This is the privilege that turns a SQL injection into a host problem. LOAD_FILE() reads anything the mysqld user can read and SELECT … INTO OUTFILE writes it back — as the server process, not as the person connecting. How far it reaches depends on secure_file_priv, which this finding names but does not measure: the setting is a separate fact, and reporting it here would be a second alarm for a finding that belongs to the server-settings suite.
SEC.PRIV.GRANT_FILE.false_positives: Almost none for an application account. A data-import job that genuinely uses LOAD DATA INFILE is the case worth checking, and it is usually better served by LOAD DATA LOCAL INFILE from the client, which needs no server-side privilege at all.

SEC.PRIV.GRANT_OPTION.bad:
-- The account can pass this on to anybody it likes.
GRANT SELECT, INSERT ON shop.* TO 'app'@'10.0.0.%' WITH GRANT OPTION;
SEC.PRIV.GRANT_OPTION.note: Every other limit on the server becomes voluntary at this point. The account can create a second one holding the same access, and the second one carries no note about where it came from — so a privilege audit run tomorrow sees a plain account rather than the path that made it. The fix keeps the account working: REVOKE GRANT OPTION FOR takes back only the ability to re-grant.
SEC.PRIV.GRANT_OPTION.false_positives: Administrative accounts hold this deliberately, and so do accounts that manage other accounts as part of their job. The finding is the list of accounts for which that should have been a decision rather than an accident — it does not claim each entry is wrong. A grant the ENGINE ships is never reported at all.

SEC.PRIV.GRANT_OPTION_STRUCTURAL.bad:
-- Not just access to the data — the power to decide what exists.
GRANT CREATE ON shop.* TO 'app'@'10.0.0.%' WITH GRANT OPTION;
SEC.PRIV.GRANT_OPTION_STRUCTURAL.note: A different sentence from its sibling rather than a worse degree of the same one. A re-grantable data privilege widens who can read or write what exists; a re-grantable structural one widens who decides what exists at all — including who can create objects that a later audit has no reason to look at twice. A migration account holding this is common and often deliberate; an application account holding it is almost never intended.
SEC.PRIV.GRANT_OPTION_STRUCTURAL.false_positives: The migration or deployment account is the legitimate case, and it is usually one account rather than several. Where the privileges genuinely belong to the account, revoking only the GRANT OPTION leaves it fully working — so the fix costs nothing even when the grant itself is correct.

SEC.PRIV.GRANT_PROCESS.bad:
-- Sees the current statement of every session on the server.
GRANT PROCESS ON *.* TO 'app'@'10.0.0.%';
SEC.PRIV.GRANT_PROCESS.note: The disclosure is the statement TEXT, not the session list. Any value interpolated into SQL rather than bound travels in it — a password being set, a token being looked up — and PROCESS shows that to this account while it runs, across every application sharing the server. Reported below FILE because it reads only what is in flight, changes nothing, and reaches nothing outside the server.
SEC.PRIV.GRANT_PROCESS.false_positives: Monitoring and observability accounts need PROCESS and are expected to hold it. The account SQLens itself connects as is never reported: this package's own setup guidance asks for a read-only audit account, and a tool that flags the privileges its documentation tells you to grant is a tool nobody trusts twice.

SEC.PRIV.GRANT_PUBLIC.note: PUBLIC is not a role somebody was given: it is the implicit membership of every role in this database, including every role created from now on. So a privilege held by PUBLIC cannot be reviewed by looking at who has access — it appears in no role listing, and the next account anybody creates has it before they ask. Grant to the role that needs the access instead.
SEC.PRIV.GRANT_PUBLIC.false_positives: PostgreSQL's own default grants — EXECUTE on functions, USAGE on the public schema in older clusters — are excluded, so an entry that reaches this rule was granted by somebody. A database that deliberately publishes a reference table to every role is the genuine exception and belongs on the ignore list with the reason written there.

SEC.PRIV.GRANT_PUBLIC_IN_MIGRATION.bad: DB::statement('GRANT SELECT ON orders TO PUBLIC');
SEC.PRIV.GRANT_PUBLIC_IN_MIGRATION.good: DB::statement('GRANT SELECT ON orders TO app_reader');
SEC.PRIV.GRANT_PUBLIC_IN_MIGRATION.note: PUBLIC is not a role somebody created — it is the membership every role in the database already has, including roles that do not exist yet. A grant to it therefore keeps widening as accounts are added, and read out of the catalog months later it is indistinguishable from a privilege somebody arranged deliberately. Grant to a named role instead, and keep the account the application connects with separate from the one that runs migrations.
SEC.PRIV.GRANT_PUBLIC_IN_MIGRATION.false_positives: GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA … TO PUBLIC is common and much less sharp than a table grant — it is still reported, because the severity is uniform and the message names the privilege so a reader can judge it. An extension's own installation script may grant to PUBLIC by design; those statements do not come through a migration and are not seen here. A role legitimately NAMED public_reader is not the pseudo-role and is not reported.

SEC.PRIV.GRANT_SCOPE_BROAD_IN_MIGRATION.note: MySQL's ON clause names a SCOPE, not an object, and two of its shapes are wildcards. `ON *.*` reaches every database on the server; `ON db.*` reaches every table in that database — including tables added long after this migration ran. A grant that keeps widening on its own is one nobody reviews again, because nothing about the next table mentions it.
SEC.PRIV.GRANT_SCOPE_BROAD_IN_MIGRATION.false_positives: A read-only analytics account over a reporting database is a legitimate use of `ON db.*`, and the statement does not say which kind of account this is. PostgreSQL never produces this finding: it has no `db.*` scope, and its nearest construct — GRANT … ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA — is a snapshot that does NOT reach tables added later.

SEC.PRIV.GRANT_SERVER_ADMIN.note: These privileges administer the SERVER rather than any one database, so they reach past the data the account was given access to: changing global settings, ending other accounts' sessions, or having the server run code as somebody else. None of that is expressible in a schema grant, and none of it shows up in a schema review. Crucially, an account does not need SUPER to be an administrator — MySQL 8.0 deprecated SUPER and split its powers across these dynamic privileges, so a check for SUPER alone comes back empty while the account holds everything that mattered.
SEC.PRIV.GRANT_SERVER_ADMIN.false_positives: A genuine DBA or backup account holds some of these on purpose and is not a defect. What the finding gives you is the list of accounts for which that was a decision — and the useful question is rarely "is this account an administrator" but "does the APPLICATION account need to be one". Privileges the engine ships are never reported, and the ability to hand a privilege on is left to the rule that owns it, so one fact is never reported twice.

SEC.PRIV.GRANT_WILDCARD_HOST_IN_MIGRATIO.note: In MySQL an account is a PAIR — the user name and the host it may connect from — and the host half is a real access control rather than a label. Removing it leaves the password carrying the whole defense: with a host restriction a leaked credential is exploitable from inside the network, without one from anywhere the server is reachable. A partial wildcard such as '10.0.%' or '%.internal' is reported too, because MySQL evaluates it as a pattern and it reads like a restriction while being wider than it looks.
SEC.PRIV.GRANT_WILDCARD_HOST_IN_MIGRATIO.false_positives: A containerized or serverless deployment often has no stable client address to name, which is a real reason to accept this id with a reason rather than to narrow the rule. The rule also reads the GRANT, not the account: a host restriction applied by a separate CREATE USER or RENAME USER statement is invisible to it. PostgreSQL is never reported — its grantees are roles, with no @host half at all.

SEC.PRIV.ROLE_BYPASSRLS.note: BYPASSRLS means every row of every table with a policy, and nothing in the policies themselves says so. If this database uses row-level security to separate tenants, an audit of the policies comes back correct and is beside the point for this account. Remove the attribute unless the role exists precisely to read across tenants.
SEC.PRIV.ROLE_BYPASSRLS.false_positives: A reporting or backup role that must read every tenant's rows is the genuine exception. As with CREATEROLE, the attribute is also reported when it is reachable through a membership — revoke the membership that leads there rather than the attribute at the end of it.

SEC.PRIV.ROLE_CREATEROLE.note: CREATEROLE lets an account create login roles and grant them access. Since PostgreSQL 16 it can no longer take privileges it does not already hold — altering a role it did not create is refused — so this is not the blanket escalation older write-ups describe. What it still is: a way to keep access outside your deployment process, with a password nobody rotates. Remove it unless creating accounts is genuinely this role's job.
SEC.PRIV.ROLE_CREATEROLE.false_positives: A provisioning or tenant-onboarding role whose job is exactly to create accounts is the expected exception. The rule also reports the attribute when it is reachable through a role MEMBERSHIP rather than held directly — that account looks unremarkable in \du, which is why the membership chain is what gets revoked, not the attribute at the end of it.

SEC.PRIV.ROLE_SUPERUSER.note: A superuser bypasses every permission check there is: row-level security does not apply to it, GRANT and REVOKE do not constrain it, and it can read and write every file the database process can. If this is the role an application connects as, every other protection in this database is advisory. Give the application a role with the privileges it actually needs, then ALTER ROLE ... NOSUPERUSER once nothing depends on it.
SEC.PRIV.ROLE_SUPERUSER.false_positives: The cluster's own bootstrap role is expected to be a superuser and is not the finding — what matters is which role the application connects as. Note that this finding stands in for SEC.PRIV.ROLE_BYPASSRLS and SEC.PRIV.ROLE_CREATEROLE: a superuser holds both by definition, so they are not reported separately for the same account.

SEC.PRIV.ROUTINE_DEFINER.bad:
-- The routine is right. This is what makes it reach further than anybody meant it to.
GRANT EXECUTE ON FUNCTION app.grant_access(bigint) TO PUBLIC;
SEC.PRIV.ROUTINE_DEFINER.note: This is the construction done RIGHT — the search path is pinned, so the escalation SEC.PRIV.ROUTINE_DEFINER_MUTABLE_PATH reports is closed here. It is listed because EXECUTE on it is a bounded loan of the owner's rights rather than an ordinary privilege: a role holding only EXECUTE can look minimal and still reach further than its other grants allow. Confirm the grant list on the routine is the one you meant.
SEC.PRIV.ROUTINE_DEFINER.false_positives: Not a defect and not reported as one — the severity is low because the finding is an inventory entry. A SECURITY DEFINER routine with a pinned path and a deliberate grant list is a correct design, and the expected outcome is that you read it and agree.

SEC.PRIV.ROUTINE_DEFINER_MUTABLE_PATH.good:
CREATE FUNCTION app.grant_access(uid bigint) RETURNS void
    LANGUAGE sql
    SECURITY DEFINER
    -- one clause, and the whole path is closed
    SET search_path = pg_catalog
AS $$
    INSERT INTO public.memberships (user_id, granted_at) VALUES (uid, pg_catalog.now());
$$;
SEC.PRIV.ROUTINE_DEFINER_MUTABLE_PATH.note: A SECURITY DEFINER routine runs as its owner, and without its own SET search_path the unqualified names inside it resolve through the CALLER's. Anyone who can create a schema and holds EXECUTE can put their own function ahead of the one it means to call — and it will be called as the owner. Pin the routine's search path: an explicit schema list, the catalog schema, or the empty string to force every name to be qualified. It changes nothing about what the routine does and closes the path entirely.
SEC.PRIV.ROUTINE_DEFINER_MUTABLE_PATH.false_positives: The presence of the SET clause is the whole test, deliberately not its value: PostgreSQL's guidance names several safe settings, and judging the value would mean maintaining a list of what counts as safe and being wrong about the first arrangement nobody thought of. What is unambiguous is the absence.

SEC.PRIV.ROUTINE_DEFINER_NO_PATH_IN_MIGR.bad: DB::statement('CREATE FUNCTION audit_totals() RETURNS void LANGUAGE plpgsql SECURITY DEFINER AS $$ BEGIN UPDATE orders SET total = 0; END $$');
SEC.PRIV.ROUTINE_DEFINER_NO_PATH_IN_MIGR.good: DB::statement('CREATE FUNCTION audit_totals() RETURNS void LANGUAGE plpgsql SECURITY DEFINER SET search_path = pg_catalog AS $$ BEGIN UPDATE public.orders SET total = 0; END $$');
SEC.PRIV.ROUTINE_DEFINER_NO_PATH_IN_MIGR.note: The routine runs with its OWNER's privileges — here, the role that runs migrations — while an unqualified name inside it resolves against the CALLER's search_path. A caller who can create an object in a schema earlier on their path therefore chooses what the privileged routine executes, and needs no injection and no bug in the function to do it. Pin the path and schema-qualify what the body touches, or declare the routine SECURITY INVOKER if it does not need the owner's rights.
SEC.PRIV.ROUTINE_DEFINER_NO_PATH_IN_MIGR.false_positives: A routine whose every reference is already schema-qualified is safe in practice and is still reported: whether the next edit stays qualified is not something the statement can promise. A pinned path satisfies this rule whatever the path says — SET search_path = public is a bad path and belongs to SEC.PRIV.ROUTINE_DEFINER_UNSAFE_PATH. MySQL routines are never reported: they are declared SQL SECURITY DEFINER and MySQL has no search_path, so the question does not exist there.

SEC.PRIV.ROUTINE_DEFINER_UNSAFE_PATH.good:
CREATE FUNCTION app.grant_access(uid bigint) RETURNS void
    LANGUAGE sql
    SECURITY DEFINER
    -- a path only the owner can write to, and pg_temp last if it is needed at all
    SET search_path = pg_catalog
AS $$
    INSERT INTO app.memberships (user_id, granted_at) VALUES (uid, pg_catalog.now());
$$;
SEC.PRIV.ROUTINE_DEFINER_UNSAFE_PATH.note: A pinned search path is not automatically a safe one. If a schema in it can be written to by anybody other than the routine's owner, the substitution the unpinned case allows is still open: a role with CREATE there defines a function under the name the routine uses unqualified, and the routine calls it as the owner. pg_temp is the second way in and needs no grant at all — it is the caller's own schema, so anywhere but last in the path it is the same gap. Point the path at a schema only the owner can write to, at pg_catalog, or at the empty string to force every name to be qualified.
SEC.PRIV.ROUTINE_DEFINER_UNSAFE_PATH.false_positives: This rule measures the catalog rather than judging the value: it asks whether any schema in the routine's own path grants CREATE to somebody other than the routine's owner. A path of pg_catalog, or of a schema only its owner may write to, produces nothing. The owner's own CREATE never counts — a routine whose owner may write to its own path is not exposed by that.

SEC.PRIV.RUNTIME_DDL.bad:
-- One grant, and every request the application serves can add an object to the schema.
GRANT CREATE ON SCHEMA app TO app_runtime;
SEC.PRIV.RUNTIME_DDL.note: The role that serves requests holds DDL, so a SQL injection reaching this connection can change the schema rather than only the rows — it can leave a table, a function or a trigger behind, which outlives the request. Note what the rule reads: PRIVILEGES, not behavior. A clean result here does not mean the application cannot be injected, only that one consequence of it is off the table.
SEC.PRIV.RUNTIME_DDL.false_positives: A project that deploys migrations on the runtime connection holds DDL by necessity, and the fix there is a second connection for migrations (SEC.PRIV.CONNECTIONS_UNSEPARATED) rather than a REVOKE that would break the next deploy — the finding says so when it detects that arrangement.

SEC.RLS.CHECK_ALWAYS_TRUE.good:
-- Either state the same condition for writes…
CREATE POLICY tenant_isolation ON orders
    USING (tenant_id = current_setting('app.tenant')::uuid)
    WITH CHECK (tenant_id = current_setting('app.tenant')::uuid);

-- …or leave WITH CHECK off entirely and let PostgreSQL reuse USING.
CREATE POLICY tenant_isolation ON orders
    USING (tenant_id = current_setting('app.tenant')::uuid);
SEC.RLS.CHECK_ALWAYS_TRUE.note: The read path is correct and the WRITE path is unchecked. A tenant sees only its own rows and can still insert or update a row carrying somebody else's id: the write succeeds, the row becomes invisible to whoever created it, and nothing reports an error. Give the check the same condition as the filter — or drop the WITH CHECK clause entirely, because PostgreSQL then applies the USING expression to writes as well, which is what almost every correct policy relies on.
SEC.RLS.CHECK_ALWAYS_TRUE.false_positives: A policy that deliberately lets a role write rows it cannot read back — an append-only ingestion path — is the real exception, and it is worth stating in the ignore entry, because the shape is indistinguishable from the mistake.

SEC.RLS.DISABLED.bad:
CREATE TABLE orders (id bigserial PRIMARY KEY, tenant_id uuid NOT NULL, total numeric);
-- listed in sqlens.security.rls.tables, and readable in full by every role with SELECT
SEC.RLS.DISABLED.note: A table that carries a tenant column and no row-level security separates tenants only as far as every query remembers to. One missing WHERE in one report — or one injection — returns every tenant's rows, and nothing in the database refuses it. ENABLE is the switch; FORCE is what makes the policies apply to the table's owner too, which is the role migrations and console sessions usually run as.
SEC.RLS.DISABLED.false_positives: A table whose tenant-shaped column means something else — a foreign key to a tenants directory that every tenant is supposed to read — is the expected exception. SQLens judges the column names it was told to treat as tenant keys, so a false positive here is a signal to narrow that configuration rather than to switch the rule off.

SEC.RLS.NOT_FORCED.good: ALTER TABLE orders FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;
SEC.RLS.NOT_FORCED.note: ENABLE alone does not apply the policies to the table's OWNER, and this audit connected as that owner — so the separation you configured is not applied to the very connection the application uses. Nothing in the policies says so: reviewing them comes back correct. FORCE removes the owner's exemption. Verify the application still returns the rows it should afterwards, because on this table it currently returns more.
SEC.RLS.NOT_FORCED.false_positives: A table whose owner is deliberately a maintenance role that must read across tenants is the genuine exception. Note the shape it leaves behind: after FORCE, the owner sees NO rows unless a policy admits it, so a maintenance job that relied on the exemption needs a policy of its own rather than the exemption back.

SEC.RLS.NO_POLICY.bad:
ALTER TABLE orders ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;
-- …and no CREATE POLICY, ever
SEC.RLS.NO_POLICY.note: Row-level security enabled with no policy at all denies every row — PostgreSQL's default is to admit nothing. Nothing is exposed; the data is simply unavailable, which is why this shape reaches production so often. Whoever created the table is its owner and sees it working, the migration passes, and the application connects as a different role and gets empty result sets with no error anywhere. Add the policy, or DISABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY until there is one.
SEC.RLS.NO_POLICY.false_positives: A table switched on ahead of the policy that is about to land in the same deploy is the benign case, and it is still worth seeing: between the two migrations the table answers nothing.

SEC.RLS.OWNER_UNRESTRICTED.good: ALTER TABLE orders FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;
SEC.RLS.OWNER_UNRESTRICTED.note: The same missing FORCE as SEC.RLS.NOT_FORCED, seen from the other side: this audit did NOT connect as the owner, so the application path is restricted as intended. But migrations, maintenance commands and console sessions usually do run as the owner, and each of those reads and writes across tenants with no policy consulted and nothing reported. Which of the two findings you get says who the audit connected as, not how bad the table is.
SEC.RLS.OWNER_UNRESTRICTED.false_positives: As with SEC.RLS.NOT_FORCED: an owner that exists precisely to work across tenants is the real exception, and after FORCE it needs an explicit policy rather than the implicit exemption.

SEC.RLS.POLICY_ALWAYS_TRUE.bad:
ALTER TABLE orders ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;
CREATE POLICY tenant_isolation ON orders USING (true);  -- placeholder that shipped
SEC.RLS.POLICY_ALWAYS_TRUE.good:
CREATE POLICY tenant_isolation ON orders
    USING (tenant_id = current_setting('app.tenant')::uuid);
SEC.RLS.POLICY_ALWAYS_TRUE.note: A policy whose USING expression is a constant true admits every row of the table to every role the policy names. The table reports row-level security as enabled and a policy as present, so every summary of this database looks correct — and the separation does not exist. Replace the filter with the tenant condition, or drop the policy if it was only there to make the table readable again.
SEC.RLS.POLICY_ALWAYS_TRUE.false_positives: A deliberately permissive policy for a lookup table that every tenant may read in full is the genuine exception. Write it as a policy naming that role rather than as USING (true) for PUBLIC, and the intent is visible to the next reader as well as to this rule.
